issues.author: karansag
issues.body:
## Symptom

At 18:34:34Z on 2026-11-20, the Iris hub's `federation-sync-cw-us-east-02a` thread crashed with `TransferBudgetExceeded` and stopped handing federated jobs to peer `cw-us-east-02a`. By 19:38–19:45Z, 47 pending jobs across 8 users were stuck on the hub in `"Awaiting acceptance by peer cw-us-east-02a"` (`PENDING_HANDOFF`, promoted on the hub but never acknowledged by `cw-us-east-02a` via `LaunchJob`), including small 8-H100 and 8-CPU jobs that fit on free cluster capacity. Direct submissions to the `cw-us-east-02a` regional controller continued to succeed. After a hub controller restart around 20:13:00Z on the same pre-fix image, the awaiting backlog drained to 0, leaving the hub exposed to recurrence.

Incident record: [Echo wiki 1035](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/1035).

## Cause evidence

- **Hub controller crash:** At 18:34:34,161Z on 2026-11-20 (`epoch_ms = 1795199674161`), hub thread `federation-sync-cw-us-east-02a` crashed with `rigging.filesystem.cross_region.TransferBudgetExceeded`: 10.00 GB already transferred plus a 13.4 MB bundle read from `gs://marin-us-central2/iris/marin/state/bundles/...` would bring the total to 10.01 GB, exceeding the 10 GB cross-region limit. No later controller log line naming `federation-sync-cw-us-east-02a` appeared up to the Finelog query time (~19:45Z).
- **Recurrence on pre-fix hub build:** This is the same crash stack as [Echo incident 982](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/982) (2026-11-13), whose fix in [PR 11399](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11399) (`aa68291f14`, merged 2026-11-17T15:42:06Z) closed [issue 11389](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11389). Hub `GetProcessStatus` (`process_info.provenance`) reports `base_commit = e9ae26899c` (2026-11-14T08:32:03Z, `tree_hash = 08b66dd6b2`, `branch = main`, `dirty = false`) — three days before [PR 11399](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11399) merged — confirming that the fix is not deployed on the running hub.

## Live observations (2026-11-20)

- **During stall (19:38–19:45Z, read-only):**
  - **Hub pending queue (all 104 pending jobs paged):** **47 jobs** across 8 distinct users showed `"Awaiting acceptance by peer cw-us-east-02a"`. The oldest awaiting job was an 8-H100 job submitted at 17:45:07Z (~2 hours pending); next oldest was submitted at 18:36:34Z, followed by a burst starting at 18:50:52Z. An 8-CPU CPU-only job submitted at 19:19:54Z was also stuck in the same state. Separately, **5 jobs** (all 64-H100 jobs) showed `"Queued for peer cw-us-east-02a to report free capacity"`.
  - **Regional controller on `cw-us-east-02a` (newest 40 root jobs inspected; timestamps are regional `submitted_at`, not accept timestamps):** The newest hub-forwarded root job (present on the hub with `peer_status = SYNCED`) was submitted at 18:33:36Z; hub-forwarded jobs were accepted from 17:45Z up to ~18:34Z, and no hub-forwarded root job submitted after ~18:34Z appeared among the newest 40 root jobs. Direct regional submission still worked (newest root job overall submitted at 19:26:36Z with no hub record).
  - **Available capacity on `cw-us-east-02a` (`kubectl`, schedulable `Ready` nodes):** **12 free H100 GPUs** across three Ready nodes (8, 3, and 1 free H100 respectively), **~1,360 free CPUs** on GPU nodes, and **~450 free CPUs** across 4 CPU-only nodes. Both the awaiting 8-H100 job and the awaiting 8-CPU job fit in idle capacity.
- **Post-restart recovery (20:19–20:21Z, read-only):**
  - Hub `GetProcessStatus` reported uptime 434.6 s at ~20:20:15Z (process started ~20:13:00Z), still on the same pre-[PR 11399](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11399) build (`e9ae26899c` / `08b66dd6b2`). Hub jobs showing `"Awaiting acceptance by peer cw-us-east-02a"` dropped from **47** to **0** (out of 61 pending total; 8 jobs showed `"Queued for peer cw-us-east-02a to report free capacity"`), with the earliest post-restart task start on `cw-us-east-02a` among the formerly stuck jobs at 20:13:19Z (no direct accept timestamp is stored; regional `submitted_at` carries hub submit time).
  - Of the 47 formerly stuck jobs, **43** appeared on `cw-us-east-02a` (22 running, 7 succeeded, 12 killed, 2 failed) and **4** were absent on `cw-us-east-02a` with hub state `KILLED` (`"Cancelled (peer reported the job gone)"`). At least **2** of the 43 (the 8-H100 and 8-CPU jobs above) were cancelled on the hub and resubmitted directly to `cw-us-east-02a` at 19:54:07Z / 19:53:35Z; the remaining **41** on `cw-us-east-02a` cannot be split between post-restart hub hand-offs and direct resubmissions from read-only controller state alone.

## Code path (checked at `main` `a9ebf7ceb0`)

- `lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/jobs.py:232-244` (`_federated_pending_reason`): `HandoffState.QUEUED_HANDOFF` renders `"Queued for peer {cluster} to report free capacity"`, whereas `PEER_STATUS_PENDING_SCHEDULING` (for a promoted `PENDING_HANDOFF` job) renders `"Awaiting acceptance by peer {cluster}"`.
- `lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/federation/store.py:39`: `PENDING_HANDOFF = 0` means persisted locally on the hub while the peer has not yet acknowledged `LaunchJob`.
- `lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/writes.py:838-864` (`promote_queued_handoff`): compare-and-set transition that promotes a job from `QUEUED_HANDOFF` to `PENDING_HANDOFF` for the chosen peer.
- `lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/federation/availability.py:270-336` (`assign_queued`, specifically lines 279, 288–289, and 335–336) and `lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/federation/manager.py:67` (`DEFAULT_MAX_HANDOFFS_PER_CYCLE = 8`): queue assignment walks candidates in priority-then-age order and skips jobs that do not fit, ruling out head-of-line queue blocking.

## Requested action

Deploy a hub controller image that includes [PR 11399](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11399) (`aa68291f14`) so bundle reads use `unbudgeted_url_to_fs` and one failed bundle read cannot kill a per-peer federation sync thread. Restarting the same pre-[PR 11399](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11399) image (`e9ae26899c` / `08b66dd6b2`) only resets the 10 GB process-wide cross-region transfer budget and leaves the hub exposed to the same recurrence once another 10 GB of cross-region bundle reads accumulate.

issues.body:
## TL;DR

Legacy Grug SFT runs under `experiments/post_training/long_loop` (PR [#11120](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11120), head `c6676c91ef`) force the step-1 restore check to a permanent checkpoint, save `keep` milestones permanently, and can write the final step twice when it is also a `keep` milestone. Across 17 dated runs on 2026-11-18 under `s3://marin-us-east-02a/tmp/ttl=30d/long-loop-436/`, this produced 43 native checkpoint prefixes totaling 24,360,070,312,426 bytes (24.36 TB), including 33 prefixes (17,887,983,830,450 bytes, 17.89 TB) in the dated non-one-hour inventory and 10 prefixes (6,472,086,481,976 bytes, 6.47 TB) in the one-hour pair. A manual cleanup deleted 27 intermediate prefixes (16,984 inventoried objects, 11,704,773,554,338 bytes, 11.70 TB of inventoried objects deleted; billed quota relief was not measured).

Most of the mechanism already exists in Levanter and Marin. PR [#5983](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/5983) added `keep_last_temporary_checkpoints`, PR [#10782](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10782) applied final-only permanent retention with rolling temporary checkpoints to `SFTSpec`, and PR [#11552](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11552) fixed forced final re-saves on `main`. Long-loop legacy Grug SFT needs four changes:

1. Use the existing `save_final_checkpoint` helper and retain `wait_until_finished()` in `sft_runtime/train.py`, and bring in PR [#11552](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11552) from `main`.
2. For an unlisted step-1 restore gate, explicitly request a temporary save through the checkpointer, run the non-forced save path, wait for commit, then load from the actual temporary destination. Preserve a named permanent step-1 milestone. The gate copy counts toward rolling retention and can be pruned after enough newer temporary commits or on a permanent commit.
3. Default `sft-smoke.yaml` and long-loop Grug SFT recipes to rolling temporary checkpoints (`keep: null`, time-based `save_interval`, `keep_last_temporary_checkpoints: 2`) plus explicit named permanent steps (`[{"every": s, "until": s}, ...]`) for export and eval milestones.
4. Remove and verify absence of `metadata.json` before deleting payload objects in `Checkpointer._do_rm_checkpoint` so subsequent discovery skips the prefix; abort payload removal if marker removal fails.

## Prior work

| Item | State | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| PR [#4457](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/4457) / Issue [#4456](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/4456) | Merged / Closed | Sets default `keep` for `default_train`, `default_sft`, and `default_dpo` to empty so only rolling temporary checkpoints and the final permanent checkpoint are kept. |
| PR [#4387](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/4387) / PR [#5066](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/5066) / Issue [#4386](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/4386) | Merged / Closed | Adds `temporary_base_path` to `CheckpointerConfig` and routes temporary checkpoints to region-local TTL temp buckets while keeping forced and step-policy saves permanent under `base_path`. |
| PR [#5945](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/5945) | Merged | Sets Grug launchers to `keep=None` (final permanent checkpoint plus temporary recovery saves). |
| PR [#5983](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/5983) | Merged | Adds `keep_last_temporary_checkpoints` to `Checkpointer` and `CheckpointerConfig`, pruning older temporary checkpoints on commit while deleting all temporary checkpoints when a permanent checkpoint commits. |
| Issue [#5386](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/5386) | Open | Tracks resume corruption paired with sparse permanent checkpoints and single-temporary retention losing 8k steps. |
| PR [#9427](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9427) | Merged | Adds on-demand permanent checkpoint requests and lowers hero temporary checkpoint TTL from 14 days to 3 days. |
| PR [#10498](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10498) / Issue [#8290](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8290) | Merged / Closed | Bounds SkyRL RL recovery checkpoints to 2 by default via `SkyRLRetentionPolicy`, protecting pending HF exports and selected best checkpoints. Long-loop RL already uses this in `experiments/post_training/long_loop/rl.py:62` (`retained: 3` in `specs/rl.yaml:4`). |
| Issue [#10453](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10453) | Open | Documents TensorStore chunk-layout failures when resuming into a root that still contains uncommitted partial checkpoint directories. |
| PR [#10774](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10774) | Merged | Commits the completed step on SIGTERM preemption before exit in Grug trainers. |
| PR [#10782](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10782) | Merged | Sets `SFTSpec.checkpointer` to `save_interval=30m`, `keep=None`, `keep_last_temporary_checkpoints=1` in `experiments/sft/launcher.py:601-605`, routing recovery saves to Marin's 14-day TTL scratch prefix. |
| PR [#11217](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11217) | Merged | Sets hero SFT (`experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/launch_hero_sft.py`) to save permanent checkpoints every 500 steps alongside hourly temporary checkpoints. |
| PR [#11552](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11552) / Issue [#11534](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11534) | Merged / Open | Makes `Checkpointer.on_step(..., force=True)` wait for and reuse a pending or committed permanent save from the same checkpointer and step instead of rewriting `step-N/`. Merged to `main` on 2026-11-17 (`bc25c57f14`), absent from PR [#11120](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11120) (`c6676c91ef`). |

## Current behavior in long-loop SFT

All line citations below refer to PR [#11120](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11120) at `c6676c91ef` unless noted as `main` (`ea1257ca8d`).

Long-loop SFT has two launch paths in `experiments/post_training/long_loop/spec_pipeline.py:122-133`:

1. Shared `SFTSpec` path (`shared_sft.py:105-122`): inherits `SFTSpec.checkpointer` from `experiments/sft/launcher.py:601-605` (PR [#10782](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10782)): 30-minute rolling temporary checkpoint (`keep_last_temporary_checkpoints=1`), `keep=None` (permanent final checkpoint only), temporary root resolved via `apply_output_path` (`lib/marin/src/marin/training/training.py:243`).
2. Legacy Grug path (`sft.py:40-85`, `sft-smoke.yaml`, `sft_runtime/train.py`), used by the 2026-11-18 Snowball ablations and the live eight-hour arms:
   - **Paths (`sft.py:53-56`)**: sets `base_path = <output>/checkpoints` and `temporary_base_path = <output>/temporary-checkpoints`. Sets `load_checkpoint = False` and `load_checkpoint_path = []`, which disables own-root resume (`experiments/grug/checkpointing.py:162-163`; an empty list also overrides `TrainerConfig.checkpoint_search_paths` at `lib/levanter/src/levanter/trainer.py:968` so auto-resume requires `load_checkpoint_path = None`).
   - **Default schedule (`sft-smoke.yaml:8059,8073-8089`)**: enables `save_checkpoints: true`, `keep: [{every: 15}]`, `save_interval: 30m`, `delete_old_temp_checkpoints: true`, `keep_last_temporary_checkpoints: 2`. Every 15th step is permanent (`is_temporary: false`) under `<output>/checkpoints/step-N`.
   - **First-step restore gate (`sft_runtime/train.py:204-217,1526-1530`)**: when `first_checkpoint_restore_step` is set (set to `1` in all 17 runs on 2026-11-18 and in the three eight-hour configs), `restore_first_checkpoint` calls `checkpointer.on_step(tree=state, step=step, force=True)` at `train.py:208` and reloads from `checkpointer.base_path` at `train.py:212`. Because `force=True` sets `my_save_permanent_ckpt = True` (`lib/levanter/src/levanter/checkpoint.py:622-623`), `step-1` is written as a permanent checkpoint in `checkpoints/step-1` and is not pruned.
   - **Per-step checkpointer call (`sft_runtime/train.py:1542`)**: calls `checkpointer.on_step(tree=state, step=current_step)`. In `Checkpointer.on_step` (`checkpoint.py:628-633`), `step % current_every == 0` takes precedence over `save_interval` and saves a permanent checkpoint under `base_path`; time-policy saves go to `temporary_base_path` with `is_temporary=True` (`checkpoint.py:652-655`).
   - **What is deleted (`checkpoint.py:659-665,718-740,768-779`)**: after a temporary checkpoint commits, rank 0 prunes older temporary checkpoints beyond `keep_last_temporary_checkpoints` via a background `fs.rm(plain_path, recursive=True)` thread. After any permanent checkpoint commits, rank 0 calls `_prune_temporary_checkpoints(0)` to delete all tracked temporary checkpoints. This pruning path only removes temporary checkpoints. The frozen inventories quantify permanent checkpoint prefixes; the cited base-start and eight-hour configs disable time-based saves, while the one-hour configs allow them at `1h`. The inventories do not establish an absence of temporary writes across all runs.
   - **Why the final save is doubled (`train.py:1542,1570-1571`, `checkpoint.py:609`)**: when the final step matches `keep`, the periodic call (`train.py:1542`) already writes it. The later forced call (`train.py:1570`) on the pinned legacy source can rewrite it because PR [#11120](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11120) lacks PR [#11552](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11552) (`main` `checkpoint.py:618-621`) and line 609 (`if step == self._last_save_step and not force: return`) does not return when `force=True`. The observed doubled finals are consistent with a second OCDBT generation in the same `step-N/` directory. Use the existing `save_final_checkpoint` helper (`checkpoint.py:756-761`) and retain `wait_until_finished()`. PR [#11552](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11552) independently makes the forced path on `main` reuse a pending or committed permanent save from the same checkpointer and step. Neither guard prevents a rewrite across a new process or resume.
   - **Other retention hooks**: `BestValidationCheckpoint` (`sft_runtime/validation_checkpoint.py:89-92`) deletes older parameter-only validation checkpoints under `eval.best_checkpoint_path` when enabled. `archive.py:100-142` (`checkpoint_cleanup`) only runs in post-archive cleanup after verified HF publication.

## 2026-11-18 storage evidence and projected savings

At 2026-11-19 01:22:06Z, shared `cw-us-east-02a` STANDARD storage reported 971,569,804,211,080 bytes used of 1,000,555,581,276,160 bytes quota (28.99 TB headroom, zone/storage-class level; receipt `048e21ad`). Across 17 dated long-loop training runs under `s3://marin-us-east-02a/tmp/ttl=30d/long-loop-436/` (excluding six post-hoc BF16 downcast roots), three frozen inventories account for 43 native checkpoint prefixes:

| Cohort (frozen snapshot) | Runs | Prefixes | Actual bytes | Superseded intermediate bytes (exact) | Failed step-1-only bytes (exact) | Doubled-final excess (est.) | Single-gen retained incl. failed-run step 1 (est.) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Dated non-one-hour inventory (`7a10d9c8`, 15 runs) | 15 | 33 | 17,887,983,830,450 (17.89 TB) | 6,988,863,920,962 (6.99 TB, 18 prefixes) | 401,190,894,951 (0.40 TB, 1 prefix) | 5,113,836,902,455 (5.11 TB, 13 finals) | 5,785,283,007,033 (5.79 TB) |
| One-hour FP32 pair (control + treatment) | 2 | 10 | 6,472,086,481,976 (6.47 TB) | 4,314,718,738,425 (4.31 TB, 8 prefixes) | 0 | 1,078,690,430,031 (1.08 TB, 2 finals) | 1,078,677,313,520 (1.08 TB) |
| Combined 2026-11-18 training cohort | 17 | 43 | 24,360,070,312,426 (24.36 TB) | 11,303,582,659,387 (11.30 TB, 26 prefixes) | 401,190,894,951 (0.40 TB, 1 prefix) | 6,192,527,332,486 (6.19 TB, 15 finals) | 6,863,960,320,553 (6.86 TB) |

Evidence fingerprints: 33-prefix inventory `7a10d9c8`, 27-prefix cleanup inventory `10f82be8`, one-hour step-15/60 inventory `ac410e45`, cleanup delete result `111df195`, quota snapshot `048e21ad`, byte-accounting artifact `daf14dfa`.

Notes on measurements and estimates:
- Measured single-save sizes on 67B Snowball: E12 FP32 runs (`params=float32`) are 539.34 GB (doubled final 1,078.68 GB, ratio 2.000); base-start BF16 runs are 401.19 GB (doubled final 802.39 GB, ratio 2.000); E12 BF16 runs are 270.33 GB (doubled final 540.66 GB, ratio 2.000). The one non-doubled completed final (`carried-replay-v9-eager` step 2, where `2 % 15 != 0`) was 270.33 GB (ratio 1.000 vs step 1).
- The 27-prefix manual delete (16,984 inventoried objects deleted, 11,704,773,554,338 bytes, 11.70 TB; billed quota relief not measured) equals the 26 superseded intermediate prefixes across the 16 completed runs (11,303,582,659,387 bytes: 16 `step-1` = 6.46 TB, 4 base-start `step-15` = 1.60 TB, 6 one-hour `step-15/30/45` = 3.24 TB) plus the 1 `step-1` prefix from the failed `base-start-20261118/control` run (401,190,894,951 bytes).
- For a doubled final we use the same run's step-1 size as a single-generation proxy. The inventories do not isolate bytes by generation.
- At a successful final commit and after pruning, the proposed policy would avoid retaining about 17.50 TB across this cohort (12.10 TB on the 33-prefix subset), assuming the listed intermediates are all dispensable. This is post-prune retained footprint, not cumulative writes or billed relief. The 0.40 TB failed-run save is included in the retained estimate until lifecycle cleanup.
- For the three live eight-hour FP32 arms (config sets `first_checkpoint_restore_step=1`, `save_interval=null`, `keep=[{every: 120, until: 240}, {every: 480, until: null}]` on a source without PR [#11552](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11552)), estimated native checkpoint storage after successful completion is 5 single-save equivalents per arm (step 1 + step 120 + step 240 + 2x step 480, about 2.70 TB per arm, 8.09 TB across three arms), excluding exports and temporary overlap. This estimate counts the forced step-1 save separately from the earlier 6.47 TB planning figure (4 saves per arm). With a temporary step-1 save and single final write, estimated post-prune native checkpoint storage drops to steps 120, 240, and 480 (3 x 539.34 GB, about 1.62 TB per arm, 4.85 TB across three arms), avoiding about 1.08 TB per arm (3.24 TB total).

## Proposed rolling-checkpoint policy

Existing PRs cover most of the design: PR [#5983](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/5983) provides rolling temporary retention (`keep_last_temporary_checkpoints`), PR [#10782](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10782) provides the `SFTSpec` default, and PR [#11552](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11552) fixes the forced final double-save on `main`. No existing PR wires these rules into the legacy Grug long-loop path or makes deletion metadata-first.

Proposed behavior for long-loop Grug SFT:

1. **Named permanent steps for export and eval**:
   - Declare milestone steps explicitly (for example `[120, 240, 480]`) and encode them for `CheckpointerConfig.keep` as `[{"every": s, "until": s} for s in sorted(set(steps))]`. Because `Checkpointer._get_current_step_save_interval` (`checkpoint.py:745`) selects the first interval with `until >= step`, for strictly increasing positive steps `s_1 < ... < s_k`, each interval `(every=s_i, until=s_i)` matches `step == s_i` and no step in `(s_{i-1}, s_i)`. No Levanter schema change is needed to represent arbitrary named steps.
   - Default `sft-smoke.yaml` and runs without named milestones to `keep: null` (final permanent checkpoint only).
2. **Rolling temporary recovery checkpoints**:
   - Set `save_interval: 30m` (or `60m` for multi-hour runs), `delete_old_temp_checkpoints: true`, and `keep_last_temporary_checkpoints: 2` for multi-hour runs (`1` for short runs where losing one interval is acceptable).
   - Route `temporary_base_path` to a same-region short-TTL prefix (for example `tmp/ttl=3d/...` matching PR [#9427](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9427), or `<output>/temporary-checkpoints` when `<output>` is already under a short TTL). Never route across regions.
   - For resumable runs, set `load_checkpoint: null` and `load_checkpoint_path: null` so `TrainerConfig.checkpoint_search_paths` searches both `base_path` and `temporary_base_path`.
3. **Temporary first-step restore gate**:
   - For an unlisted step-1 restore gate, explicitly request a temporary save through the checkpointer (`request_checkpoint(CheckpointRetention.TEMPORARY)`), run the non-forced `on_step` path, wait for commit, then load from the actual temporary destination (`temporary_base_path or base_path`). Preserve a named permanent step-1 milestone. The gate copy counts toward rolling retention and can be pruned after enough newer temporary commits or on a permanent commit.
4. **Single final permanent write**:
   - Use the existing `save_final_checkpoint` helper and retain `wait_until_finished()` at `sft_runtime/train.py:1570-1571`, and bring in PR [#11552](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11552) from `main` so the forced path also reuses a pending or committed permanent save from the same checkpointer and step.

## Risks and mitigations

| Risk | Mechanism | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|
| Resume while a delete is in progress or crashed mid-delete | `Checkpointer._do_rm_checkpoint` (`checkpoint.py:768-779`) runs `fs.rm(plain_path, recursive=True)` on a background thread. Recursive removal may delete data objects before the metadata marker. If a process dies mid-delete, `metadata.json` can remain while payload objects are missing. Resume fallback (`experiments/grug/checkpointing.py:184`) only catches `FileNotFoundError`, so a TensorStore read failure aborts resume. | Remove and verify absence of `metadata.json` before deleting payload objects so subsequent discovery (`checkpoint.py:1249-1250`, `checkpointing.py:86-88`) skips the prefix. Abort payload removal if marker removal fails. This does not protect a reader that already selected the checkpoint. Keep writes and deletes to a reused step prefix serialized. |
| Selection file naming a rolled or deleted step | External scripts or mismatched `selected.json` files can point to an intermediate step that was later pruned (seen on 2026-11-18 when two historical one-hour `selected.json` files pointed to `step-15`). | Keep temporary checkpoints strictly in `temporary-checkpoints/` with `is_temporary: true` and permanent milestones in `checkpoints/` with `is_temporary: false`. Preserve and enforce the `is_temporary is False` guard in `sft.py:75,95` and `shared_sft.py:142` across all export, eval, and selection writers so no selection file can bind a temporary checkpoint. Declare export/eval steps in `keep` upfront. |
| Uncommitted partial checkpoint directories on resume | Issue [#10453](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10453): a crash mid-save leaves partial TensorStore files without `metadata.json`; re-saving that step after resume can fail with a chunk-layout mismatch. | Rolling retention does not prevent this. Keep `temporary_base_path` on a short TTL and track [#10453](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10453) separately (or clean uncommitted dirs above the restored step on resume). |
| Transient peak storage above `N` checkpoints | Commit-before-prune holds `N` retained copies while writing the next save. One in-flight save can temporarily add a third 539 GB copy (about 1.62 TB for two retained copies plus one write), before permanent milestones and any delete backlog. Async deletion can lag or fail, so this is not a hard peak bound. | Size storage headroom gates for `N + 1` temporary saves plus planned permanent milestones and delete-backlog margin, or set `N = 1` when headroom is tight. |
| Failed runs leaving orphaned temporary checkpoints | If a run dies before committing a permanent checkpoint and is not resumed, `_prune_temporary_checkpoints` never runs again. | Place `temporary_base_path` under a same-region short TTL prefix (`tmp/ttl=3d/` or `tmp/ttl=14d/`) so orphaned temporary checkpoints expire automatically. |

## Open decisions

1. Default `keep_last_temporary_checkpoints` for multi-hour long-loop SFT runs: `2` (one extra retained copy of about 539 GB in FP32) or `1` (matches `SFTSpec` default in PR [#10782](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10782)).
2. Keep `first_checkpoint_restore_step = 1` as a temporary save on every run, or restrict it to smoke/qualification runs.
3. Land the `metadata.json`-first deletion fix in `lib/levanter/src/levanter/checkpoint.py` on `main` separately from the legacy long-loop change against the prototype branch (`benfeuer/long-loop-prototype`).

comments.body:
🤖 Measured result: the doubled final save cost about 0.54 TB per eight-hour run (November 19, UTC).

## What happened

Two eight-hour Snowball SFT runs (480 updates each, from 10/05) wrote their final step-480 checkpoint twice. In the control run, the step-480 prefix held 1,271 objects and 1.079 TB, which is two full writes. About 0.54 TB of it is not referenced by the checkpoint manifest. The second run (single-use) showed the same doubled step-480 write. The one-hour runs showed the same pattern at their final step 60.

## Cause

At the end of training, `sft_runtime/train.py` calls `checkpointer.on_step(..., force=True)`. In this branch, `on_step` skips a same-step save only when `force=False`. So the forced final call writes a second version of a step that was already saved. Readers are not affected, because they read through `manifest.ocdbt`. The old data files stay in storage, unreferenced.

## Fix

Commit `6164fcbd` replaces the forced `on_step` call with `save_final_checkpoint` and adds a test in `lib/levanter/tests/test_checkpoint.py`. Its code was reviewed. It is in [PR 11737](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11737). Runs from the pre-train base launched today use this source. Runs already launched from the earlier source were not changed.

issues.author: karansag
issues.body:
Marina cannot serve a named app publicly. An app with `name` in `applet.toml` (for example EvalDash, served at a host such as `evaldash.oa.dev`) is always behind Marina's authentication. `marina release --mode public` fails with "Named applications are private; public applets use the isolated applet origin" ([`applets.py:562`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/fb9ef1e6e9/infra/marina/src/marina/applets.py#L562-L563)). `marina apps mode UUID public` fails with "Named applications remain private" ([`applets.py:911`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/fb9ef1e6e9/infra/marina/src/marina/applets.py#L909-L915)). A bound named host also stays authenticated (`infra/marina/README.md`, "Named app hosts").

Today a public app must be unnamed. It is then served only at `https://public.applets.marina.oa.dev/a/<uuid>/`, and it loses the features that require a name: data URLs, scheduled jobs and agent panels. For example, the Snowball family tree (#10719) can stay public only as an unnamed app at a UUID URL.

Done when: a checked-in named app, deployed from `main`, can be released in public mode and served read-only without sign-in on its own hostname. Write routes, SQL, publication and MCP must stay private, as they are for public applets today.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖
## Research

Named public release and mode changes are rejected in [`applets.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/fb9ef1e6e9c41159f047e69b455389a6739e6280/infra/marina/src/marina/applets.py#L558-L563) and [`set_mode`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/fb9ef1e6e9c41159f047e69b455389a6739e6280/infra/marina/src/marina/applets.py#L904-L920). The [public service](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/fb9ef1e6e9c41159f047e69b455389a6739e6280/infra/marina/src/marina/server.py#L244-L256) admits only `/a/*` GET/HEAD requests; [named routes](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/fb9ef1e6e9c41159f047e69b455389a6739e6280/infra/marina/src/marina/server.py#L1297-L1368) require authentication, and [Pulumi](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/fb9ef1e6e9c41159f047e69b455389a6739e6280/infra/marina/__main__.py#L377-L389) maps every configured named host to the authenticated service. PR #10829 uses an unnamed public applet and does not change these gates.

## Proposed Fix

1. Add an explicit public named-host inventory to Marina configuration and Pulumi. Map those hosts to the existing unauthenticated reader service; keep private named hosts on the IAP service. Resolve each public hostname through `applet_hosts` and return 404 for an unbound, archived, or private app, checking the current mode on every request.
2. Serve only the bound app's root, assets, `data/` files, and GET/HEAD backend routes on its public hostname, with anonymous identity. Preserve revision redirects and cache revalidation after host rebinds. Keep SQL, publication, mode changes, MCP, other Marina control routes, and mutating methods unavailable on the public service.
3. Remove the named/public rejection from release and mode changes once that route gate is in place. Report the bound public hostname in release and mode responses, falling back to the public UUID URL until a host is bound. Update the Marina README with the release, binding, and revocation steps.
4. Add regression tests for public named release and mode changes; anonymous page, asset, data, and API reads; 404s for private, archived, unbound, and cross-app host requests; and rejection of writes and control routes. Check the Pulumi domain mapping in preview before rollout. Review the app's GET handlers before publication because Marina cannot prove they have no side effects.

issues.author: karansag
issues.body:
Queries on the Finelog `log` table that filter on `epoch_ms` open every file. The catalog does not record each segment's time range, so the time filter cannot skip any file. Most of the query time goes to reading Parquet footers, not data. That is why day-sized scans exceed the 10-second query deadline. #11087 raises that deadline to 30 seconds as a stopgap. Once time-filtered queries can skip files, the deadline can go back down.

## Evidence

A one-hour `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` on the `marin` hub (2026-11-08 23:38 UTC). It filtered `epoch_ms` to one hour, plus `LIKE` filters on `key` and `data`. Wall time was 7.1 s. Full query, plan and metrics: https://gist.github.com/karansag/160e31066556f7b00199c6b328d925f5

Table: `log` in namespace `marin`, 10.4 B rows, 324 GB, 1,977 segments. Trigram indexes on `key` and `data`. No sort columns and no partitioning.

| metric | value |
|---|---|
| files pruned by statistics | 1.66 K total, 1.66 K matched: **0 files skipped** |
| row groups pruned by footer stats | 2.49 K total, 6 matched |
| bytes scanned | 5.00 MB |
| `metadata_load_time` | 18.23 s |
| `time_elapsed_opening` | 52.41 s |
| output rows | 9 |

The times are summed across 16 parallel file groups, so they exceed the wall time.

The catalog records each segment's `seq` and `key` ranges, but not `epoch_ms`. So every file's footer is read just to get the `epoch_ms` min and max. After that, the query reads almost nothing: 6 row groups and 5 MB.

Impact: a 60-day pull of `levanter.model_cache` lines in 12-hour windows lost 58% of its windows to `snapshot read deadline exceeded`, even with three retries per window (#9233).

## Possible directions

- Record per-segment `epoch_ms` min and max in the catalog, so time filters drop files before they are opened.
- Sort or cluster segments by time during compaction, so those ranges are narrow.

## Done when

- A one-hour `epoch_ms` query on `log` opens only the segments that overlap that hour.
- The default query deadline can go back to 10 seconds, reverting #11087's increase.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 # Research

`Store::query_providers` snapshots paths only, and `NamespaceProvider` gives every path to DataFusion before the existing row-group and index pruning runs. Neither the in-memory segment record nor the SQLite catalog carries `epoch_ms` bounds. This matches the issue's one-hour plan: 1,660 files matched file statistics, then only six row groups were read.

**Relevant code**
- [`store.rs#L515-L527`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/finelog/rust/src/store/store.rs#L515-L527) — snapshots paths for query providers
- [`provider.rs#L112-L182`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/finelog/rust/src/query/provider.rs#L112-L182) — registers all paths before scan
- [`catalog.rs#L193-L207`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/finelog/rust/src/store/catalog.rs#L193-L207) — persisted segment columns
- [`namespace.rs#L735-L759`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/finelog/rust/src/store/namespace.rs#L735-L759) — flush publishes segment metadata
- [`executor.rs#L318-L334`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/finelog/rust/src/store/compaction/executor.rs#L318-L334) — compaction creates replacement metadata

# Proposed Fix

1. Measure the min/max `epoch_ms` span of current `log` segments and the overlap count for representative one-hour and one-day windows. The existing L1+ sort is by `(key, seq)`, so wide time spans could leave most files overlapping even after catalog pruning.
2. Add nullable `min_epoch_ms` and `max_epoch_ms` to the segment catalog and in-memory segment metadata. Migrate existing SQLite catalogs; derive bounds for new L0 segments from the sealed batch, carry correct bounds through compaction and level bumps, and backfill old/adopted segments from Parquet footers. A bound is usable only when every row group has complete statistics. Missing or incomplete bounds keep the segment in the scan.
3. Include bounds in the same snapshot as segment paths. For safe conjunctive `epoch_ms` comparisons, intersect the time range with those bounds and pass only overlapping paths to `ListingTable`, before DataFusion footer reads and before trigram/exact pruning. Keep the SQL predicate as a residual filter; do not infer time from `seq` or file creation time.
4. Test results and planned file groups with multiple segments, out-of-order timestamps, an old catalog, missing statistics, restart/adoption, and compaction. Benchmark the same one-hour query after backfill with maintenance quiescent. Record files opened, footer load time, and wall time; lower the raised query deadline only after representative day scans fit under 10 seconds.

No open PR found for segment time pruning. #11086 and #11087 address the deadline only. If step 1 shows most segments overlap each window, time-aware segment layout needs a separate design: changing the current `(key, seq)` layout or seq-contiguous compaction can break existing pruning and segment identity assumptions.

comments.author: HRL9000
comments.body:
🤖 **Design: in-catalog min/max bounds for declared columns, like key bounds**

This matches **proposed fix 2** in the [research comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11172#issuecomment-6773719532): per-segment `epoch_ms` bounds in the catalog, filled at write, carried through compaction and level bumps, and backfilled from footers. A segment without bounds stays in the scan. Two notes on the other fixes there:

- **Fix 1 (measure segment time spans) is done: the measurements are below.** Segments are already narrow in time: across all ~1,940 live `log` files the median spans 0.5 h, p99 8.7 h and the maximum 33 h. Replaying this issue's hour against per-file bounds keeps 2 files out of ~1,660. Details are under Background below.
- **Fix 3 is more general than the snapshot detail.** The general requirement is that the query engine uses the segments' min/max statistics correctly before opening files; carrying bounds with the segment paths is one way to do that. DataFusion can already skip files from per-file statistics it is given; today Finelog gives it none from the catalog, so it has to read every footer to find them.

The design follows. It covers background, proposal, success criteria, approach, rollout, timeframe and alternatives.

### Background and Motivation

A one-hour query on `log` is slow because Finelog opens almost every file in the table to find the few that hold that hour.

- **The query.** An `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` of a one-hour `log` search opened about 1,660 files, and the `epoch_ms` filter pruned none of them. After the footers were read, only 6 row groups and 5 MB were scanned. Three hub reports for similar searches show 2,313–2,379 candidate files and 6.8–8.7 s each.
- **Why the `epoch_ms` filter pruned no file.** Before it opens files, Finelog can drop a segment by its key-column bounds, its `seq` bounds or its partition. For `log` the `epoch_ms` filter matches none of these. `log`'s key column is `key` (the log source, a string), so the catalog has no `epoch_ms` bounds, and `log` is not partitioned. The key column does two jobs, sort order and catalog bounds, and `log` chose `key` for fast per-source reads.
- **Pruning by `epoch_ms` min/max would be effective, because each file covers a short time span.** `log` has about 1,940 live files. The median file spans 0.5 h, p99 8.7 h, maximum 33 h. With per-file `epoch_ms` min/max in the catalog, the issue's hour would keep 2 files instead of about 1,660.

### Proposal

Today the catalog keeps min/max bounds for one column per table, the key column (key bounds), and query planning prunes segments by them. This proposal lets a table declare more columns that get the same in-catalog bounds. They become part of the segment list that the server keeps in memory for each table, so planning drops a segment before it opens the file, with no footer read.

- **Opt-in per column.** Bounds on every column would fit (an estimated 12–39 MB on top of about 60 MB of catalog), but most columns do not prune: each file covers nearly their full range.
- **Start with time columns.** About 65 bytes per segment: about 0.7 MB for the whole hub (about 1% of the catalog).

#### Which tables benefit

Files still opened for a window from the lookback start until now, with the share skipped:

| Table | GiB | Files | Time column | 1h | 6h | 1d | 7d | Needs |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `log` | 302.7 | 1,935 | `epoch_ms` INT64 | 62 (97%) | 69 (96%) | 103 (95%) | 169 (91%) | step 1 |
| `iris.worker` | 27.5 | 233 | `ts` | 51 (78%) | 53 (77%) | 54 (77%) | 62 (73%) | steps 1, 2 |
| `zephyr.worker` | 14.2 | 185 | `ts` | 29 (84%) | 41 (78%) | 60 (68%) | 67 (64%) | steps 1, 2 |
| `iris.task` | 11.0 | 327 | `ts` | 63 (81%) | 80 (76%) | 90 (72%) | 106 (68%) | steps 1, 2 |
| `iris.profile` | 7.7 | 155 | `captured_at` | 17 (89%) | 19 (88%) | 30 (81%) | 34 (78%) | steps 1, 2 |

- **Already pruned by time:** `levanter.metrics`, `telemetry_v1.node_agent`, `telemetry_v1.marinskyrl` and `telemetry_v1.vllm` (332 GiB). Their key is `timestamp_ms`, which is `INT64`, and the Grafana queries filter it with integer literals (`timestamp_ms >= {start_ms}`). Those filters reach the key-bound check today.
- The issue's hour was in the past, so only compacted files overlap it (2). A window ending now also keeps the 30–60 recent files that are not compacted yet, which is why the 1h column shows 62 for `log`. By bytes, the skip is 97% or more through 1d.

### Success

Success is achieved when:

1. On the hub, the issue's one-hour `log` query opens fewer than 100 files instead of about 1,660–2,370.
2. `iris.task` and `iris.worker` show the same kind of drop for one-hour `ts` filters.
3. Query results never change. The first implementation has tests that check this while bounds are absent or partial: a table where no segment has bounds yet, a mix of segments with and without bounds (as during the backfill), and the same after the backfill. Each test asserts that a time-filtered query returns exactly the rows it returns with pruning turned off.

Wall time is measured but is not a gate, because the exact cause of the 7 s is still open.

### Approach

**Step 1: bounds on `log`** (success 1 and 3)

1. Add a `catalog_bounds` column flag to the table spec, and set it on `log`'s `epoch_ms`.
2. Store each flagged column's min and max per segment in the catalog. Fill them when Finelog writes a segment.
3. Add a maintenance task that reads the footers of existing segments once and fills their bounds. Most of `log` is never rewritten, so this is needed.
4. In planning, drop a segment when its bounds do not overlap the filter's range. Always scan a segment with no bounds, so results cannot change.
5. Also read the `extract(epoch from now())` filter form that `lib/finelog/OPS.md` documents. Change `lib/finelog/OPS.md` to integer literals.

**Step 2: timestamp columns** (success 2 and 3)

6. Teach planning to read timestamp literals (`ts >= TIMESTAMP '...'`, `ts > now() - INTERVAL '1 hour'`). Planning ignores them today.
7. Set the flag on `iris.task`, `iris.worker`, `iris.profile` and `zephyr.worker`.

### Rollout

Each step deploys to `marin-dev`, then the three CoreWeave servers, then the hub. Each deploy is approved separately. Before the hub deploy, record a baseline of the issue's one-hour query.

### Expected Timeframe

- Step 1: about 1 week to a reviewed PR, then 1–2 days to deploy.
- Step 2: about 3 days to a reviewed PR, then 1 day to deploy.

### Alternatives Considered

| Option | Why not |
|---|---|
| **Leave it in place.** Add a `seq` range to time-bounded queries. | Works today, but a user must first find the `seq` range for a time. |
| **Larger footer and index caches.** | The hub reports show 12–36 footer reads for about 2,300 files and about 7,080 index cache hits: the caches were warm and the queries were still slow. A cache also empties at each restart and must grow with the table's history. |
| **Partition `log` by time.** | Finelog has no time transform, partition selection needs exact values (`=`, `IN`), and the query side does not read a table's own partition spec. A `day` column would change every writer and query and need a rewrite of about 325 GB. |
| **Make `epoch_ms` the key column of `log`.** | The `key` bounds make per-source reads (`key = ...`) fast, which is `log`'s main read path. Keeping `key` as the sort order would need an explicit sort setting, which is part of the source layout and so rewrites the table. |

`log.epoch_ms` is already flagged in #11394.

The hub's query log agrees as far as it goes. Finelog writes a `read execution report` record for every failed or cancelled read and for every successful read that takes 7 s or more. The log doesn't survive a container recreate, so it covered only about the last 2 hours:

| Table | Range filter | Outcome | Count | p50 / max | Files scanned (sum) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `telemetry_v1.node_agent` | `timestamp_ms` | ok | 4 | 8.5 / 10.1 s | 219 |
| `iris.task` | `ts` | ok | 1 | 9.4 s | 258 |
| `iris.task` | `ts` | failed at planning | 1 | 27 ms | 0 |
| `storage.usage` | none | ok | 1 | 9.6 s | 100 |
| `telemetry_v1.zephyr` | `timestamp_ms` and another column | ok | 1 | 7.9 s | 21 |

There were no cancelled reads in the window. Files scanned counts the candidate segments that reached the scan. For `node_agent` that was about 55 per query.

Left out:

- `iris.task`, `iris.task_state`, `iris.task_event`, `iris.worker`, `iris.provisioning` and `zephyr.shuffle` are range-filtered on `ts`, which is a timestamp column, and the feature covers INT64 columns only. The `iris.task` query above scanned the most files in the window, so covering timestamp columns would be a separate change worth considering.
- `telemetry_v1.zephyr.timestamp_ms` is already the key column, so key bounds already cover it. Flagging it would add nothing for its slow query above.
- `storage.usage`'s slow query has no range filter, so bounds wouldn't help it.
- Tables with fewer than about 200 segments have little to prune.

In local tests, turning the flag on for one of these tables was a metadata-only change: registering the flagged schema published a new table spec version that took effect immediately, with no rewrite of existing data. That held for unsorted, sorted, row-group-capped and partitioned object-backed tables. The production specs weren't read, and a table whose spec sets a physical layout different from its schema's own sort and row-group settings could still need a rewrite.

Two gaps remain:

- The evidence is thin: eight records from about 2 hours. A follow-up should keep these records across container recreates, so the next list can rest on a longer window.
- How much time one segment spans is not measured yet. With `seq` as the key, segments follow arrival order, so each should cover a short span. Forwarding lag and merges into the largest level can widen that.

They copy the SQL that Finelog logs for slow FetchLogs reads: a `key` prefix filter for the job, `seq > 0`, an `epoch_ms` range, `ORDER BY seq DESC LIMIT 50000`. issues.author: penfever
issues.body:
## TL;DR

Two long-loop recipes produced opposite SFT→RL changes on the Micro210 panel. Mochi `.123` (SFT step 400407 → RL final step 22) went from **59.74% to 52.91% pooled (−6.82 pp)** and **68.39% to 58.90% on the 19-benchmark mean (−9.49 pp)** under Micro210 policy `2026.11.20-together` (`8f7ef817`). Snowball long-loop round 1 (SFT 746 → RL 16) went from **40.23% to 45.26% pooled (+5.03 pp)** and **47.98% to 52.16% on the 20-benchmark mean (+4.18 pp)** under its earlier MiniMax-judge policy. Both runs are "Exp1" of their respective series: the first Mochi RL run and the first Snowball long-loop round ([#11337](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11337)). The two comparisons differ in base model, SFT recipe and length, RL pool composition, optimizer and learning rate, batch geometry, checkpoint selection, eval policy, judge and serving stack. Each delta is a sealed observation under its own frozen policy; the pair is not a causal RL comparison.

## Description

This issue records both sides of the comparison from primary evidence: the sealed Micro210 evaluations in [#11337](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11337), the Mochi reward curves in [#12119](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/12119), the SFT mix history in [#12199](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/12199), and the two RL recipes (`specs/rl.yaml` at `0c1e81ca93` for round 1; `rounds/mochi-throughput-train-track1.yaml` on `benfeuer/long-loop-prototype` plus the `.123` resolved launch for Mochi).

Micro210 is 200 tasks across 20 benchmarks expanded to 440 attempt slots (AIME24 and OlympiadBench ×10, GPQA/TBLite/TB2 ×3, others ×1). Scores are heterogeneous partial-credit reward means, not pass@1. Missing grades are absent, not zeros ([#10197](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10197)).

### Setup side by side

| Setting | Mochi `.123` | Snowball round 1 (Exp1) |

### The RL mixes are not identical

Both runs draw from the same two release families — `.123`'s curriculum pins `swe-verified-20261112-v4` (`ec645c79…`) and `smartie-mixed-20261110-v1` (`94f21b06…`), the same pins round 1 consumed — but the mixes differ in four ways. First, the agentic share: round 1 admitted 32 agentic + 32 nonagentic groups per update (50%); `.123` consumed 11 + 21 of 32 (34.4%), matching the Exp4 curriculum's 35% agentic target. Second, `.123` adds `nemotron_if` (a curated retained pool of 54,953 rows) at 15% of groups; round 1 has no Nemotron instruction-following source. Third, the sampler: round 1 drew uniformly within each route pool; `.123` used the domain-weighted sampler with pass-variance weighting and adaptive exploration. Fourth, the pools themselves: round 1 consumed the releases' parquets directly; `.123` consumed the Exp4-family stamped pools (`rl-pools/2026.11.22.2`), re-versioned with grader-fixed source versions. The six nonagentic sources keep identical group shares by construction: round 1's uniform-within-pool expectation is each source's row share × 0.5, which is exactly `.123`'s curriculum weight.

## Hypothesis or Goal

Question: did the same kind of SFT→RL recipe improve Snowball and hurt Mochi? Goal: put both sealed results side by side, identify which design differences could produce opposite deltas, and state what would de-confound the comparison.

## Confounds

Ordered by how much they could move the headline deltas.

1. **The RL mixes differ** (table above): agentic share 50% → 34.4%, a new `nemotron_if` source at 15%, uniform vs pass-variance-weighted sampling with adaptive exploration, and different pool materializations. The Exp4-ancestor pools also carry grader-fixed source versions relative to the parquets round 1 consumed.
2. **Different Micro210 policies and harnesses.** Round 1's rows use the MiniMax-M3 judge policy; Mochi's use `8f7ef817` (GLM-5.3-Flash). Cross-model score levels are not comparable, and even round 1's two evals ran on different harness generations (pre- vs post-repair, different serving geometry). Only within-model deltas are meaningful here.
3. **Optimizer and learning rate.** Mochi trained with MuonH at LR 1e-5 (adam_lr 2.31e-6 for its non-Muon parameters) with clipping disabled; round 1 used AdamW at LR 1e-6 with max_grad_norm 0.5 — a 10× learning-rate difference and a different optimizer family. [#12103](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/12103) plans exactly this ablation for both models.
4. **Different base models and SFT recipes.** Mochi: a different base lineage with a 6,916-update full-A/B hero SFT (special-token LR ×5.66, linear LR). Snowball: the 262K base with a 746-update long-loop mix on the 10/05 full-AB stores plus 20% replay. Starting-point capability differs enormously: under the same GLM policy, Mochi SFT pools 59.7% while round 1's SFT 746 was never evaluated under it (its MiniMax-policy score is 40.2%).
5. **Steps, wall-clock and stop reason.** Round 1 completed 17 updates and died at update-18 admission inside a 12 h budget; `.123` completed 22 updates and stopped on its 10 h wall budget with max_steps 32 unused. Different amounts of RL pressure on different schedules.
6. **Checkpoint selection.** Round 1 published an EMA-best checkpoint under a fully-covered 120/120 validation gate. `.123`'s holdout never reached the 180/200 scored eligibility bar (165–176/200 across all evals), so its published checkpoint is the fallback final step 22, not a validated best. Its own curves ([#12119](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/12119)) show training reward rising (0.547 → 0.713 by update 17) while holdout pass@1 fell from baseline (0.679 → 0.665 at update 15) — the selection rule could not rescue this because coverage, not score, failed the gate.
7. **Eval defects and coverage asymmetries.** Mochi's CRUXEval RL cell is a grader artifact worth −70 pp (#11922); excluding it shrinks the regression from −9.49 to −6.13 pp. TruthfulQA is nearly uninformative (#12060) and moved +10 pp for Mochi but −20 pp for round 1. BixBench is ungraded for Mochi (10 `ValueError` attempts without verifier grades; the credential-guard defect is [#12094](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/12094)) but was scored (0.00 → 0.20) under round 1's policy. Mochi's pooled means use different valid populations (413 vs 428); round 1's use 420 vs 439 scored with different harness generations.
8. **Tiny per-benchmark samples.** Ten distinct tasks per benchmark (100 for AIME24/OlympiadBench, 30 for GPQA/TBLite/TB2); one task moves a 10-task cell by 10 pp, and repeated attempts are not independent tasks.
9. **Serving stacks.** Training and eval ran on different hardware and parallelism (GB200 DP16/EP16 TP1 vs H100 TP1/PP2/CP5/EP8; 5 vs 22 rollout engines; different context windows), which changes rollout distributions and eval reproducibility.
10. **Known policy-reward limitations on shared sources.** Typed `PolicyRewardMeasurement` receipts landed with the first Snowball measurements (`ba083af95a`), including the Smartie finish-task weakness and an empty-think-block effect that depresses the measured reward on the Smartie source. Both runs consume that source at the same expected share (5.8% of groups), but through different samplers, so the limitation enters both training signals differently.

## What this does and doesn't show

Does show: two sealed within-model SFT→RL deltas under each run's own frozen policy; the full design differences; that Mochi's regression survives excluding the defective CRUXEval cell (−7.08 pp on the 17-cell panel); and that the matched-mix analogs (Exp3/Exp4) exist but lack SFT-only baselines.

Does not show: that RL causally helps Snowball and hurts Mochi; any cross-model score comparison (different judges and policies); or that step 22 is Mochi's best available checkpoint (it is a fallback selected by coverage failure).

De-confounding, in order of leverage:
1. Run the same RL pool and recipe on both models — `.123` already trains on the Exp4 pool family, so an SFT-only Micro210 eval of the Exp4 (or Exp3) SFT checkpoint under a common policy would give a matched-mix delta on the Snowball side.
2. Re-evaluate both selected checkpoints on the repaired Micro210 policy `2026.11.23-together` now in flight ([#12069](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/12069): CRUXEval frozen graders #11922, TruthfulQA option shuffle #12060, IFBench checker #11926, BixBench judge relay #12094, Pi MCP adapter #12122, provisioning #11787), with a reference rescore to quantify per-cell policy effects.
3. The optimizer/LR ablation planned in [#12103](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/12103).
4. Paired per-prompt comparison of holdout updates on shared scored tasks, as proposed on [#12119](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/12119).

Filer links require Marina login; raw `s3://` paths appear inline beside each link.

## Decision Log

* Comparator: Snowball long-loop round 1 (SFT 746 → RL 16), per the 2026-11-24 user ruling, replacing the initially proposed Exp5 pairing. Exp5 remains as context because it is the only Snowball run evaluated under the same GLM policy as Mochi, but it uses a different RL curriculum (`exp5-rl@2026.11.20`).
* Analog: Exp4 is named the closest matched-RL-mix run because `.123`'s curriculum identity is `long-loop/exp4-rl@2026.11.18`; Exp3 is the near match. Neither has an SFT-only Micro210 eval, so no matched-mix SFT→RL delta is reported and none was launched (read-only task).
* `.123`'s batch is 32 groups × 8 samples (256 trajectories/update) per its resolved launch (`train_batch_size: 32`) and logged `consumed/sequences: 256` per update.
* Pool-count provenance: the per-source table uses the round-1 release manifests and `.123`'s curriculum weights; the materialized `rl-pools/2026.11.22.2` manifest is the source of truth for exact counts and was not readable in the drafting session.

## Conclusion

Round 1's +5.03 pp pooled / +4.18 pp benchmark-mean gain and `.123`'s −6.82 pp pooled / −9.49 pp mean drop are real sealed observations, each under its own frozen eval policy. Every layer that could produce the difference also differs: RL mix and sampler, optimizer and learning rate, base model and SFT recipe, run length and stop reason, checkpoint selection, eval policy and harness, and one Mochi eval cell that is a grader defect worth −70 pp. The records support "opposite deltas, heavily confounded" — not "RL helps Snowball and hurts Mochi". The matched-pool SFT-only baselines (Exp3/Exp4) and the repaired Micro210 policy re-evaluation are the cheapest next measurements.

issues.author: chrismc91
issues.body:
Evalchemy-derived benchmarks package their scorers through two name-keyed registries: `source_package` in [`importers/evalchemy/grader.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/taskcompendium/src/taskcompendium/importers/evalchemy/grader.py), and a copy in `fewshot_grader.py`. Each has a `DEPENDENCIES` table and a dispatcher (`scorers/main.py`, `scorers/fewshot.py`); 13 files call them 17 times. `scorer_revision` hashes `grader.py` and ships `main.py` with every scorer, so any registry edit gives every one of those corpora a new name and a rebuild. That has happened 10 times since 2026-11-03, mostly when a benchmark was added (LEXam #11778, FACTS Grounding #11753, LongBench v2 #11504, GenomeQA #10984).

The helpers in [`convert/script_grader.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/taskcompendium/src/taskcompendium/convert/script_grader.py) (`grade_script`, `shipped_files`, `script_package`) already package one grade script per benchmark for LiveCodeBench, ARC, Lean and Nemotron Ultra. Judged scorers that report several metrics need a verdict-file reward, blank answers passed to the scorer, and a judge contract. `script_package` supports none of these, so FrontierScience Research (#11887) builds its `ScriptGrader` by hand. `script_package` should keep its stdout contract, because the Harbor export only converts stdout-reward graders (`harbor_export.py:311`).

Proposed shape: a separate `verdict_package(files, config, *, environment, timeout, judge=None)` beside `script_package`, plus `files_revision(files)` for recipe versions. Each benchmark module declares its grade script and shared scorer modules once. Logic now in `scorers/main.py` moves into the scorer modules: Olympiad's judge fallback, FACTS Grounding's judge inputs and IFEval's spec construction. IFBench's directory tree needs a `shipped_files` equivalent for directories.

Migrate every caller in one PR. A partial migration still edits `grader.py`, which renames the remaining corpora again. Every migrated corpus gets a new identity whether or not its scores change. Coordinate with #11756: build its judge-access contract on `verdict_package` instead of `source_package`.

Done when:
- `verdict_package` and `files_revision` exist, and FrontierScience Research uses them.
- Every `source_package` caller ships its own grade script, and `grader.py`, `fewshot_grader.py`, `scorers/main.py` and `scorers/fewshot.py` are deleted.
- The import-closure test in `test_evalchemy_math.py` checks each benchmark's declared files, not `DEPENDENCIES`.
- Re-grading stored answers gives identical rewards and metrics for a sample of migrated benchmarks, including one judged and one Olympiad.

issues.author: WhenWen
issues.body:
Opened on behalf of @WhenWen for the belay-wn research loop. Updates are posted here as results land.

**Question.** Why does MuonH (fixed-norm hyperball matrices) trail MuonW on KMA d768 fast_track? Can a weight-normalized optimizer beat a *fairly tuned* MuonW-family baseline? The work covers KMA d768 and the Belay ladder recipe (d512–d1280, plus the 8-minute d512 speedrun). All numbers are Paloma macro loss, and gaps under the 0.005 band count as ties.

**Current answer (2026-11-19).** With equal tuning, the weight-normalized forms tie tuned MuonC. Neither family leads anywhere.
- *Baseline.* The bar is MuonC (Defazio, arXiv 2506.02285): MuonW with matrix decay λ·lr_t/lr_max and an AdamW head. Its decay is tuned per length: best λ is 0.2–0.4 on the speedrun, 0.2 at ladder d512, and about 0.1 at d768. Both families also use the same s(t)² head anneal and late matrix anneal ("tl-d schedule").
- *Speedrun, d512, 8 min.* nonsi (learned per-matrix radius on MuonH) + schedule, with its starting size tuned, against tuned MuonC + schedule: +0.0007 over nine held-out seeds (95% −0.0033 to +0.0046). Both beat the recipe's MuonH by about 0.011–0.016.
- *Ladder d512.* nonsi + schedule against MuonC (λ 0.2) + schedule: +0.0033 on fresh seeds 4–7, a tie.
- *Formula-cap ball.* A no-decay ball whose per-layer cap comes from a shape/LR law, with no retuning. It ties MuonC + schedule on all four rungs: −0.0031, −0.0011, +0.0048 and −0.0029, one seed each. It also ties on the speedrun (+0.0004 over six seeds).
- *Mechanism.* Loss is set first by rotation per step and second by how matrix size evolves, not by where size ends up. A fit on MuonC's settings alone predicts nonsi's loss from its rotation to within 0.002. The original MuonH–MuonW gap fits the same picture: MuonH's rotation and size were off the optimum.
- *Open: d1280.* softcap + schedule (tl-d) trails MuonC + schedule by 0.0158 on one seed. Running d1024 width on d1280's recipe does not reproduce this, and a second seed is running.

**Intake posts.** speedrun-track proposals for nonsi + schedule (#9514, comment 7019355085) and MuonC (λ 0.2) + schedule (#9514, comment 7019433555).

**Running now**
- An "unnormalized hyperball" baseline: MuonH's norm-relative step with no projection, plus MuonC- or MuonW-style decay. It is tuned like MuonC and becomes the bar wherever it wins.
- MuonC decay brackets at d768–d1280.
- nonsi + schedule at d768–d1280, with seed 2.
- A second d1280 seed for tl-d vs MuonC + schedule.

Runs log to W&B project `understanding-sam/research-loop-belay-wn`.

comments.author: WhenWen
comments.body:
🤖 **Experiment log, part 1 of 3: the KMA d768 gap and the first weight-normalized fixes (2026-11-17)**

Setup: KMA d768 fast_track, batch 128, ctx 4096, 6,930 updates, 8×H100. Metric: final validation loss on the tuning split (plus a fixed held-out set once it was verified). Seeds are paired.

**Baselines reproduced**
- MuonW seeds 0/1/3: 2.51555 / 2.51564 / 2.5219 (four-seed mean 2.5182).
- MuonH seeds 0/1/2: 2.52054 / 2.52530 / 2.52428.
- Mean paired gap +0.0057 (+0.0064 over three paired seeds). On the fixed held-out set it is +0.0054, lower bound > 0.
- MuonW LR ×0.71 / ×1.41 is worse than ×1.
- Checkpoint restore is bitwise exact on H100, and interrupted-vs-uninterrupted continuation matches.

**Where the gap is** (log reads and swap runs)
- MuonH's deficit is front-loaded: +1.8 nats in the first 100 steps, about 0 by step 5000, then a ~0.006 loss in the final anneal.
- Swaps put the whole gap in the hidden-matrix update:
  - MuonW matrices + MuonH head/Adam groups: 2.5164.
  - MuonH matrices + MuonW Adam groups: 2.5218.
  - Gates and fallbacks don't matter.
- Rotation vs size, finals:
  - ShadowH (MuonW's rotation on fixed spheres) ends at MuonH's level: best 2.5273, ×0.5 2.5360, ×2 2.5441.
  - MuonH's rotation with MuonW's size law ends at 2.5112 / 2.5138.
  - So the gap is weight scale, not rotation.
- MuonW for the first 1,000 steps, then MuonH holding those sizes: 2.5078. MuonH's problem is mainly its first ~1,000 steps at the small init size.

**Candidates (MuonH step + some way to set the matrix size)**
- *Fixed bigger spheres* at 0.66× the update size: 2.5178 (seed 0), equal to MuonW's mean.
- *C2* (radius follows MuonW's size law in closed form): 2.5112 / 2.5138 on seeds 0–1. On held-out it is −0.006 / −0.003 vs MuonW.
- *C3* (grow by that law for 1,000 steps, then hold) on seeds 1–5:
  - −0.0057 vs original MuonW.
  - −0.0024 vs tuned MuonW (not claimed).
- *Radial MuonH* (learned log-radius per slice, Adam on ⟨G, W⟩):
  - 2.5047 / 2.5082 on seeds 0–1, about 0.01 below MuonW.
  - But radii ran away up to ~4,600× on slices whose output feeds a norm. Their radial gradient is rounding noise, and Adam with ε≈0 turns it into full steps.
- *softcap* (outward radius steps scaled by 1 − (s/c)², c = 2, capped at 7.4×):
  - Kept all of radial's gain: seeds 0–1 mean 2.5060. Any cap from 2.5× to 15× gives the same result, and 1.5× loses it.
  - Against the original MuonW on seeds 2–7: −0.0091 (bound −0.0056), held-out −0.012.
- *nonsi* (no learned radius on the scale-invariant slices, no cap):
  - Seeds 0–1 mean 2.5064.
  - Learning radii for only the first 500 steps keeps almost all of the gain (2.5084).
- Closed negatives:
  - gradient-gated or slower learned sizes: ~2.517
  - coupled learned size: 2.544–2.552
  - adaptive step rules: 2.62–2.67
  - persistence: 2.520

comments.author: WhenWen
comments.body:
🤖 **Experiment log, part 2 of 3: stronger baselines, the speedrun and the ladder (2026-11-17 → 11-19)**

**The MuonW bar gets tuned, and most of the d768 lead goes away**
- *Tuned MuonW* (step 1.41×, matrix decay 0.05, no decay on head/small params): seeds 0–1 mean 2.5100. Most of the original H–W gap came from this.
- *Head step.* MuonW also gains from a smaller AdamW head step (0.18–0.35× all within 0.001). Against head-tuned MuonW, softcap's d768 lead is about 0.0001–0.001.
- *tl-a / tl-d* (softcap plus an extra s(t) factor on the head step, plus a late matrix-angle anneal ∝ s² from 79.4% of training): tl-d reached 2.4969 on seed 0.
  - MuonW given the same anneals: 2.5000 (head anneal −0.0056, both anneals −0.0070).
  - So the anneal gain is generic.
- *MuonC* (Defazio, arXiv 2506.02285: MuonW whose matrix decay is λ·lr_t/lr_max):
  - Default head: 2.5011 (s0).
  - Head-tuned: 2.4944 (s0) / 2.4982 (s1).
  - With tl-d's anneals: 2.4943 / 2.4994, beating tl-d by 0.0027 / 0.0020.
  - Decay grid at d768: 0.1 is best (0.15 +0.0016, 0.2 +0.0055, 0.3 +0.0165, 0.4 +0.0278).
- *Pre-registered confirmation* (seeds 2–11, Holm over five candidates):
  - softcap and nonsi pass against the tuned MuonW defined beforehand: −0.0044 (p 0.006) and −0.0043 (p 0.005).

🤖 **Experiment log, part 3 of 3: new weight-normalized forms, the mechanism, and what is running (2026-11-18 → 11-19)**

**Forms that did not beat MuonC (KMA d768, two seeds, same commit unless noted)**
- *Weight-normalized MuonC* (radius follows MuonC's decay law): 2.5121 / 2.5148, which is +0.011 vs MuonC. Changing decay moved the size 5× but the loss only ≤ 0.004.
- *ShadowC* (MuonC's rotation on a sphere): 2.5189 at init radius. With softcap's learned radius it gets 2.5086 (λ0.1), still worse than plain softcap.
- *Learned gain on MuonC* (MuonW family): adds nothing (+0.0007 to +0.0034). A weight-normalized head on MuonC's matrices costs about 0.
- *Four new constraint shapes, all with interior LR brackets:*
  - spectral-norm sphere: 2.4994, ties tl-d, −0.0018 behind MuonC + schedule
  - capped ball: +0.0020 vs tl-d
  - per-row radii: +0.0030 vs tl-d
  - Stiefel/orthogonal: about 0.10 worse; the constraint was verified exact, so this is real
- *Per-family caps* on the formula-cap ball: no gain (−0.0008 to +0.0092). *Caps at a fixed multiple of init:* best +0.003 vs the law cap.

**Forms that tie MuonC**
- *Formula-cap ball* (no decay; per-layer cap = 0.71·√(39·lr_max/(2·0.1))·|U_l|):
  - KMA d768: 2.4978 vs MuonC + schedule 2.4967.
  - Belay ladder vs same-commit MuonC (λ0.1) + schedule: −0.0031 / −0.0011 / +0.0048 / −0.0029 (d512–d1280).
  - Speedrun: +0.0004 over six seeds vs MuonC λ0.4.
  - It beats tl-d by 0.018 at d1280.
- *Ball capped at MuonC's measured final sizes* (explanation only): 2.49695 vs 2.49694.

**Mechanism, measured**
- Rotation per step is the first variable. Across MuonC and nonsi settings it explains loss with R² 0.97 on the ladder; final matrix size explains 0.02. A fit on MuonC's settings alone predicts nonsi's loss to within 0.002.
- Size is second, and it is the path over training that matters, not the end point:
  - Pinning nonsi at MuonC's final per-layer sizes loses ~0.009.
  - nonsi at start ×4 ends at MuonC's size with the same rotation and is 0.008 worse.
- In this recipe MuonC's matrices grow toward a fixed per-layer size and hold, without shrinking late.
- The formula-cap ball behaves like MuonC at about 1.2× its nominal decay, which is why its larger cap ties and its smaller cap loses.
- tl-d's d1280 loss is not radius stranding; tl-d's radii there are larger than softcap's. d1024 width on d1280's recipe does not reproduce it: nonsi + schedule and MuonC + schedule both score 2.3478 there.
- The original KMA H–W gap fits the same picture: MuonH's rotation and its size path were away from the optimum early on.

**Running now**
- *Unnormalized hyperball (uhs).* MuonH's step relative to the current norm (MuonH's tuned angular step, no projection), plus MuonC- or MuonW-style decay, with MuonC's AdamW head (0.35×, s² anneal in the schedule cells). Decay is bracketed per rung around its own balance point. Speedrun first, then the ladder. It replaces MuonC as a rung's bar if it wins.
- *MuonC decay brackets:* λ0.05 at d768; λ0.2 at d1024/d1280, run as H100 and GB200 sets.
- *nonsi + schedule:* d1024/d1280, seed 2, and d1280 head-only / anneal-only splits.
- *d1280 seed 2* for tl-d vs MuonC + schedule.
- *Formula-cap ball:* no-schedule pair at d1280.

All comparisons are now scored on the same hardware type. A difference between hardware types is only allowed as a difference of same-hardware differences.

🤖 **Update, 2026-11-19 23:25 → 11-20 00:45 PST**

**Goal change.** The target is now a weight-normalized optimizer that *beats* tuned MuonC + the s² anneals; a tie no longer counts. New lines should be designs derived from the measured mechanism, not new grids on existing forms (tuning only as much as a fair comparison needs).

The law-cap ball held at d1280 (−0.0029), so it is the only weight-normalized form that has kept pace on every rung. New designs will be confirmed on it.
- **Train-vs-Paloma offset (tdg, 308 speedrun runs, 260 pairs):** weight-normalized forms trail MuonC 0.005–0.008 more on training loss than on Paloma. This tracks the head's end size and logit scale (R² 0.75–0.80), not matrix size (0.15) or rotation (0.23), and is spread evenly over the 16 Paloma domains. It is a head trait, not a cost of weight normalization, and no held-out gain is hidden behind it.
- **Momentum echo (derivation, then a check):** each Muon update points back along its own recent steps through momentum, so ⟨Ô, Ŵ⟩ ≈ −κθ with κ ≈ 10.7. This accounts for the radial drift of the unnormalized hyperball and for the KDA w_beta runaway. It predicted the d512-ladder neutral decay at 0.152; the smoke run measured 0.166.
- **Direction noise (KMA d768):** about 80% of each Muon step goes along the momentum's noise-like directions, which hold only ~20% of its energy.
