comments.author: XiaoyuanWang111
comments.body:
🤖

Track: custom

Rerun the recipe with no flag on competitive-d1024 and competitive-d1280 from this week's branch (seed 0, each Track's own command). Then judge finished ladders against the mean of that run and the s7n run at each rung.

Every competitive rung compares a variant with one finished run (`s7n-d1024`, `s7n-d1280L16`). `belay_s7.py` says the s7n runs were trained on `marin_belay_v1_fp8quality` at `a5a8647840`, which is not an ancestor of the weekly branches. The registry still labels these baselines "(same commit, seed 0)", from the template in `registry_entry.py` line 257.

To first order, `ladder_projection` gives Δ_hero = −0.533·Δd512 − 0.115·Δd768 + 0.434·Δd1024 + 0.980·Δd1280. This reproduces the six recorded projections. A baseline offset at d1280 therefore passes almost fully into every ladder's verdict.

In the six finished ladders (X0014, X0073, X0221, X0226, X0235, X0237), the mean Δ is −0.0134, −0.0093, −0.0079 and −0.0010 from d512 to d1280. From d1024 to d1280, Δ moves toward zero in all six (mean +0.0069); from d768 to d1024 it moves +0.0014. The seed-1 recipe runs in #11785 are +0.0016, +0.0027, −0.0031 and +0.0043 relative to s7n, with the same signs at d1024 and d1280. Measured against them, the d1280 drop disappears and every projection moves by −0.0017. #11785 also found that an apparent d512 lead of −0.0045 was cross-commit noise once rerun on the same commit; the s7n baselines are cross-commit by construction.

A d1280 rerun 0.003 or more above 2.2706 would mean that every ladder's d1280 Δ is biased toward a loss by that amount. A rerun within 0.001 of it rules this out. The d1280 rung also differs from d1024 in batch (1,024 sequences, the hero's tokens per step), steps (20,023 against 39,210) and depth (16 layers), so the rerun separates the baseline from those changes.

Budget: two runs, about 1,010 minutes on one node (d1024) and 1,003 minutes on four nodes (d1280), using the run times on the Belay page.

comments.author: XiaoyuanWang111
comments.body: 🤖 Thanks for running X0254. The [report](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/marin_belay_v1_registry/experiments/belay/analysis/X0254/report.md) reads d1280 alone: 2.2716 against 2.2706 for `s7n-d1280L16`, +0.0010, inconclusive. The d1024 rerun finished at 2.4095 against 2.4106 for s7n, an offset of -0.0011 in the other direction. With both reruns as the baseline, the ladder rule's weights (+0.43 at d1024, +0.98 at d1280) move every projection by about -0.0005. None of the seven complete ladders (X0014, X0073, X0221, X0226, X0235, X0237, X0238) changes verdict, and each projection stays at least 0.0017 from the ±0.005 edges. So at these two rungs the s7n baseline from the other commit holds to about 0.001, and I see no need to rerun d512 and d768.

comments.author: WhenWen
comments.body:
Track: speedrun

**Try debiased sampled softmax so the d512 recipe can train on more tokens per GPU-second.** Compute a cheap vocabulary-shortlist loss at every training position, always including its target token. Split each sequence into blocks of 16 positions and sample one position per block. At that position compute the recipe’s full-vocabulary loss and add the difference from the shortlist loss, divided by the position’s sampling probability. Give every position positive probability, stop gradients through those probabilities, and apply the recipe’s token weights and normalization. In expectation this recovers the full training-loss gradient, including gradients to the output weights. Use exact full-vocabulary loss for Paloma evaluation.

The starting settings come from a frozen 4-layer, width-128 LM with a 128,256-token vocabulary. We used a 16,384-row shortlist and 64 full-vocabulary positions per 1,024-token sequence. On one GPU the native full-head batch of 8 took 53.8 ms. The corrected head at batch 128 took 44.1 ms and had 6.96% of that batch-8 gradient variance. Both batch size and head computation changed in this comparison. It motivates testing whether the throughput gain translates to lower validation loss on Belay. [Frozen-checkpoint measurements](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/gradient-variance-frontier/runs/8e66d762264394)

For Belay, start with a shortlist of roughly one eighth of its vocabulary and the same one-in-16 correction rate. Compare against the current fused head at equal training tokens first, then spend the measured throughput gain on more tokens in the 8-minute run. Report tokens/sec and full-vocabulary Paloma macro loss for both. Submitted with Codex assistance.

comments.author: armorfaye
comments.body:
🤖 Posted on behalf of @armorfaye.

Track: ladder

Follow-up to X0250's per-rung matrix decay ladder: put the Adam-side decays on the same timescale rule. X0250's ladder holds lambda * lr_max * N fixed for the matrices, but its Adam-side decay coefficients are constants, so their total decay over the run (coefficient * adam_lr_max * N) grows about 2x from d512 to d1024, and token_embed ends progressively smaller relative to the baseline's at larger rungs.

Keep X0250's ladder exactly (the per-rung matrix lambda from lambda * lr_max * N held at its d512-rung value, the late matrix anneal, the s(t)^2 AdamC head with lambda_h = 25 * lr_hmax / 2) and change two coefficients per rung. Let A = adam_lr_max * N, the Adam group's peak LR times the number of steps, and A_d512 its value at the d512 rung (about 33.5). (1) The MoE router weights and token_embed keep Adam's update with decay (adam_lr_t^2 / adam_lr_max) * c * W, with c = 0.3 * A_d512 / A_rung instead of the constant 0.3. (2) The other rank >= 2 Adam leaves keep AdamW with decoupled decay 0.05 * A_d512 / A_rung instead of the constant 0.05. That gives about 0.3 / 0.175 / 0.147 / 0.199 and 0.05 / 0.029 / 0.025 / 0.033 at d512 / d768 / d1024 / d1280. The d512 rung is identical to X0250's d512 rung, so it can be reused. No new parameters or state.

comments.author: armorfaye
comments.body:
🤖 Posted on behalf of @armorfaye.

Track: speedrun

Follow-up to X0250: keep X0250 exactly and change one thing, the end of the late matrix anneal. X0250's matrix LR after t0 = round(0.7937 * N) is lr_m(t) = lr_t * s(t) / s(t0), with s(t) = lr_t / lr_max, so it ends at (min_lr_ratio^2 / s(t0)) * lr_max, a third or less of the schedule's own floor, and the matrices nearly stop training over the last few percent of the run. Clamp it from below at the schedule's floor: lr_m(t) = max(lr_t * s(t) / s(t0), min_lr_ratio * lr_max). The matrix decay keeps lambda_t = lambda * lr_m(t) / lr_max with lambda = 0.2, so it follows the clamped LR. Everything else is X0250's: the MuonH-group and KDA write-strength matrices step W <- W - lr_m(t) * (O + lambda_t * W) with no sphere projection; lm_head / output_proj use AdamC at the s(t)^2 head LR with lambda_h = 25 * lr_hmax / 2; the MoE router weights and token_embed keep Adam's update with decay (adam_lr_t^2 / adam_lr_max) * 0.3 * W; the other rank >= 2 Adam leaves keep AdamW decay 0.05. No new parameters or state. Target step time equal to X0250.

comments.author: RavnaBergsndot
comments.body:
Track: speedrun

Compare the benefits of different activation control methods for the lm_head part, whether these benefits are repetitive or complementary, then decide which combination to use.
There are binary design choices for each of them:
A. vanilla rmsnorm vs gatednorm, before applying lm_head
B. raw results vs tanh capped results, after applying lm_head
C. without z-loss vs with z-loss, for the lm_head outputs
So there are 2^3=8 possibilities in the whole design space.

Rationale: There are inconsistent results on whether gatednorm-for-lm-head/tanh cap/z-loss-for-lm-head is beneficial at all, across the arch hill climbing history, and I suspect it's because sometimes one of the features here is used with the other, and sometimes it is not. So I suggest that it's time we figure this out with more clarity.

comments.author: WhenWen
comments.body:
🤖 Posted on behalf of @WhenWen.

Track: speedrun

**Law-cap ball (X0253) for the matrices, with X0250's AdamC head and Adam-side decays.** This is optimizer-only. The head stores one scalar per slice, and nothing else is added.

**Update rule** (s(t) = lr_t / lr_max of the recipe's MuonH schedule, N = number of steps, t₀ = round(0.7937 · N))
1. *Matrices (X0253).* Every MuonH-group and KDA write-strength slice takes W′ = W − η_t U. If ‖W′‖_F > cap_l, W′ is rescaled onto the ball; otherwise it is kept as is. There is no decay and no projection inside the ball.
   - U is MuonH's Newton–Schulz direction, with the √max(1, fan_out / fan_in) scale.
   - η_t is the recipe's MuonH LR. From t₀ it is multiplied by s(t) / s(t₀). KDA write-strength keeps its 2× LR.
   - cap_l = κ · √(n · min(in, out) · max(1, out/in)), with κ = √(39 · lr_max / (2 · 0.2)) and lr_max the rung's own MuonH peak. The same formula applies at every rung; nothing is tuned per rung.
2. *Head (X0250).* lm_head / output_proj use AdamC instead of AdamH. For each slice, store r0 = ‖W‖_F at init, take U = the Adam direction normalized per slice, and update W ← W − lr_h(t) · r0 · U − (lr_h(t)² / lr_hmax) · λ_h · W, with no projection. Here lr_h(t) = lr_hmax · s(t)² and λ_h = 25 · lr_hmax / 2.
3. *Router and token embedding (X0250).* The MoE router matrices (not the router bias, not attn_gate) and token_embed keep Adam's update, with decay (adam_lr_t² / adam_lr_max) · 0.3 · W. This replaces the annealed router decay.
4. *Other Adam leaves (X0250).* Rank ≥ 2 leaves get AdamW decay 0.05.

Compared with X0250, only step 1 changes: the ball replaces the schedule-scaled matrix decay. Compared with X0253, only steps 2–4 change.

**Why**
- *Ladder, same control and seed 0.* X0250 is −0.0178 / −0.0130 at d512 / d768. X0253 is −0.0077 / −0.0106 / −0.0092 / −0.0073 at d512 / d768 / d1024 / d1280.
- *Our own runs.* The ball ties MuonC with the same two anneals on every rung (−0.003 to +0.005, seed 1) and on the speedrun (6 seeds). So X0250's extra lead over X0253 likely comes from its head and Adam-side decays, which X0253 did not have. On the speedrun, X0250 (AdamC head) beats X0247 (the same matrices with an AdamW head) by 0.006.
- *No per-rung matrix decay.* The cap comes from shape and peak LR alone, so the matrices need no λ and no per-rung λ rule.

**Prediction:** on the speedrun, within ±0.005 of X0250 (−0.0203). If it ties there, the ladder is the real test: X0250 needs its per-rung λ rule at d1024 / d1280, and this does not.

spillover_issues.title: Marin Belay Intake

spillover_issues.author: gonzalobenegas
spillover_issues.body:
## What

The release contains **119 tasks**. We have Qwen3.8-27B grades for **118/119**. Marin’s Pi 0.87.0 run at xhigh (65,536-token context, 16,384-token reply cap) solved **23/118 (19.49%)**. The authors’ Claude Code run solved **35/118 (29.66%)** on those same IDs. The paired difference (Marin minus authors) was **-10.17 percentage points** (paired SE 3.88 points, approximate 95% interval -17.77 to -2.57). This interval describes variation across tasks for these two runs. We have one model outcome per task and harness. [Authors’ per-task grades](https://github.com/swescience/swescience.github.io/blob/f16153e5c47c46b2f6f2ebf0aaefae34bdf8c8bd/data/task-matrix.json)

| Outcome on the same task | Tasks |
| --- | ---: |
| Both solved | 18 |
| Marin Pi only | 5 |
| Authors’ Claude Code only | 17 |
| Neither solved | 78 |

The outcomes agreed on 96/118 (81.36%). Tasks 026, 035, 101, and 102 each received reward 0, extending the earlier 23/114 result. Task 002 retains its positive native regrade from its reconstructed patch. Task 019 (pycisTopic) remains on hold pending permission and is excluded from both denominators. The Marin grades come from the research run with Daytona verification. The leaderboard used a different harness and inference setup. These independent runs cannot isolate the contribution of either difference. [Earlier results and regrade provenance](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/12108#issuecomment-7144059476)

<details><summary>Task IDs with different outcomes</summary>

- Marin Pi only (5): 002, 009, 058, 103, 116.
- Authors’ Claude Code only (17): 004, 007, 015, 025, 026, 038, 053, 061, 062, 063, 074, 077, 080, 091, 101, 107, 112.

</details>

**Same-patch replay on 17 Qwen3.8-27B tasks.** We froze the first graded patch available for each of 17 distinct tasks and replayed it through Marin without model calls. On all 17, Marin collected the same patch bytes (SHA-256) and reproduced the standalone Pier public and private test reports and reward. Both verifiers scored 7 solved and 10 unsolved. On these same IDs, the authors’ independent model run solved 9. The outcomes agreed on 15/17 IDs. Only 004 and 007 differed: the authors solved both, while our patches passed 0/15 and 5/6 private tests respectively under both verifiers. This establishes verifier agreement on the frozen sample. The sample was selected by archive availability and does not estimate full-benchmark model performance. [Published task matrix](https://github.com/swescience/swescience.github.io/blob/f16153e5c47c46b2f6f2ebf0aaefae34bdf8c8bd/data/task-matrix.json)

**Catalog fidelity.** At PR commit `d1e8497`, all 119 compiled tasks matched the pinned release byte for byte on the instruction, and all 119 matched on solver and verifier image digests and both timeouts. Each item used Pi 0.87.0 at xhigh with a 65,536-token context and a 16,384-token reply cap. Marin requests 10 GiB of solver disk for each task. Upstream declares 20 GiB for each. The focused tests passed (17 passed, two deselected), and the named CLI dry-run resolved. [Pinned source](https://huggingface.co/datasets/OpenMOSS-Team/SWE-bench-Science/tree/997408298e8e4d09978b1120b95c4540d1a71bcb/tasks) · [Conversion and dry-run](https://iris.oa.dev/#/job/%2Fexedev%2Fswe12109-full119-convert)

**Catalog launch smoke.** At PR commit `d1e8497`, Marin’s evaluation CLI launched `swebench-science --limit 1` with the pinned Qwen3.8-27B preset. It selected task 001. Pi 0.87.0 produced a patch in the Daytona solver, and the catalog’s evaluator-worker verifier assigned reward **0**. The run record reported success and `cli scores` read back **1/1 selected task scored** from the 119-task corpus. The in-cluster launcher used the peer’s Iris client and a mounted Daytona credential. The 118-task research result above retains its original grade for task 001. [PR commit](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/d1e8497b47274a7c69dd0fe483983a6d07fc6468)

The release’s collection hook exports the patch to a fresh verifier image, which rebuilds the software and runs the private tests. Each task earns 1 when all applicable private tests pass and 0 otherwise. [Pinned task selection](https://huggingface.co/datasets/OpenMOSS-Team/SWE-bench-Science/blob/997408298e8e4d09978b1120b95c4540d1a71bcb/selections/default-96.json) · [Implementation PR](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/12109)

## Why

A scientific-code repair has to preserve the behavior checked by the repository’s private tests. This benchmark lets Marin compare models on that end-to-end task with the same harness, repositories, and grading rule. [Upstream benchmark](https://swescience.github.io/)

## Validation evidence

The Qwen3.8-27B reproduction preset pins the checkpoint, tokenizer, four-H100 serving topology and provider options. The benchmark PR uses the shared Pi runner. The Qwen-specific top-level effort override is preserved with the preset on the reproduction branch. The 114-task research run used its previously submitted workspace snapshot. [Pinned model preset](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/a6b2b398cf019fdfa0cc129e7cefc97ffe37fa5e/experiments/evaluation/serve/models/Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B-Pi-xhigh.yaml) · [Pinned request handling](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/a6b2b398cf019fdfa0cc129e7cefc97ffe37fa5e/lib/marin/src/marin/rollouts/evaluation.py#L566-L578)

The upstream default manifest and the earlier 96-task validation agree on all task IDs. The initial conversion check found byte-identical instructions, matching image digests for all 96 solver/verifier pairs, and unchanged native timeouts. The release contains a further 23 tasks that require a restricted-license opt-in. [Pinned source and image declarations](https://huggingface.co/datasets/OpenMOSS-Team/SWE-bench-Science/tree/997408298e8e4d09978b1120b95c4540d1a71bcb/tasks)

The two completed runs used mini-swe-agent with a 32,768-token context and an 8,192-token reply cap. Each model received one native grade per task.

| Qwen3.6-35B-A3B | 96/96 | 5 | 5.21% |
| Nemotron 3.5 Super VL 120B-A12B | 96/96 | 7 | 7.29% |

Both validation runs used Daytona for solver and verifier with 2 CPUs, 8 GiB RAM, and 10 GiB disk per sandbox. The release requests 20 GiB disk. The catalog uses the validated 10 GiB solver allocation and runs the verifier on its evaluator worker. Upstream’s leaderboard covers 119 tasks and uses several harnesses, which limits direct score comparisons. [Leaderboard](https://swescience.github.io/)

The full runs used the development adapter. On review head `1d1c12efc6`, focused tests cover the 10 GiB solver request, nested package selection, patch collection, verifier image references, and reward parsing. Russell’s #11664 merged. PR #12109 uses its solver-only harness installation. The completed 114-task run used the previously submitted research snapshot. Default-suite adoption is a separate decision. **Same-patch replay.** On task 009, Marin and the standalone upstream Pier 0.3.0 runner each collected a patch with SHA-256 `b3ddf0be168d420135072fb14b06b8363e7feff7285a14fd7b39cfcb929d435b`. **Matched Qwen3.8-27B harness comparison.** Marin ran Pi 0.87.0 and Mini-SWE-Agent 2.1.0 with the same checkpoint (`37561816e66b5b9153b1b64c10968c18c1e6f4a0`), 32,768-token context, 8,192-token reply limit, explicit `xhigh`, and native task verifiers. ACS publishes the underlying authors’ supplementary material under CC BY-NC 4.0. These facts support using the existing library privately with attribution. A separate redistribution grant for every downstream parameter file remains unverified. [Pinned files](https://github.com/marrink-lab/polyply_1.0/tree/160e9707d844ad1b108e1d8184152050d16088a0/polyply/data/2016H66) · [Packaging](https://github.com/marrink-lab/polyply_1.0/blob/160e9707d844ad1b108e1d8184152050d16088a0/setup.py#L40-L43) · [Polyply paper](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-021-27627-4) · [ACS supplementary material and license](https://acs.figshare.com/articles/journal_contribution/A_GROMOS-Compatible_Force_Field_for_Small_Organic_Molecules_in_the_Condensed_Phase_The_2016H66_Parameter_Set/3475124) |

**Scope of the hosted scoring run.** The catalog has 119 tasks. This review supports 118 for private, noncommercial research scoring with Marin-served inference, retaining notices and reporting aggregate results. Task 019 remains open. The previous run covered 114. The runner makes working copies: Daytona stores image layers for the sandbox, and Marin passes a source-bearing candidate patch to the verifier. Public reporting of scores publishes none of those files. This decision does not cover publication of images, raw trajectories, patches, or data. Marin already registers FinanceBench and CMMLU for evaluation. Both publishers specify CC BY-NC 4.0. These are precedents for this evaluation purpose, not blanket clearance for other uses. [Runner implementation](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/d066a47b1a/experiments/evaluation/benchmarks/swebench_science.py) · [Marin FinanceBench](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/d066a47b1a/experiments/evaluation/benchmarks/financebench.py#L28-L52) · [FinanceBench terms](https://huggingface.co/datasets/PatronusAI/financebench/blob/e04404e3a97f69f79c14d42f24981a1c9c3bcd18/README.md) · [Marin CMMLU](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/d066a47b1a/experiments/evals/task_configs.py#L524) · [CMMLU terms](https://huggingface.co/datasets/haonan-li/cmmlu/blob/efcc940752ea4a1ea94d2727f11f83858d64fc8e/README.md)

**Provider terms for the earlier OpenRouter comparison.** Daytona’s public terms limit its customer-content license to providing the service. OpenRouter’s public terms (§§6.1, 6.5–6.6) cover service operations and anonymized metrics, include sublicensing rights, and ask the submitter to have the necessary permissions. The earlier hosted Claude Code 27B comparison pinned Chutes with no fallback and did not explicitly request zero retention. At review time the exact model/provider pair did not appear in OpenRouter’s public zero-retention list. Actual account-level settings and any negotiated agreement remain unverified. Private execution with source-bearing prompts sent to a provider and publication of a numerical score are distinct uses. This review does not establish that GPL-family licenses prohibit hosted inference. [Daytona terms](https://www.daytona.io/terms-of-service) · [OpenRouter terms](https://openrouter.ai/terms) · [Provider retention policy](https://www.chutes.ai/privacy) · [OpenRouter zero-retention endpoints](https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/endpoints/zdr) · [Pinned task manifest](https://huggingface.co/datasets/OpenMOSS-Team/SWE-bench-Science/blob/997408298e8e4d09978b1120b95c4540d1a71bcb/data/tasks.csv)

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖
# Research

PR #11664 is the prerequisite for this catalog entry and remains open. Its curated Harbor path already has mini-swe-agent and separate verifier machines, but the package stager scans only top-level Hugging Face directories and the importer rejects task schema 1.3. The SWE-bench Science release places tasks under `tasks/task_###`, selects 96 unrestricted tasks, and uses `pre_artifacts.sh` to produce the candidate patch; the current importer does not run that hook.

**Relevant code**
- [#11664 `agentic.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/b5b451ed5e7c8a716696ea6a053b60b40bee9f65/experiments/evaluation/benchmarks/agentic.py#L296-L355): mini-swe-agent catalog pattern.
- [#11664 `harbor_packages.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/b5b451ed5e7c8a716696ea6a053b60b40bee9f65/experiments/post_training/task_curation/harbor_packages.py#L50-L60): top-level package discovery.
- [#11664 `config.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/b5b451ed5e7c8a716696ea6a053b60b40bee9f65/lib/taskcompendium/src/taskcompendium/importers/harbor/config.py#L18): supported schemas.
- [#11664 `package.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/b5b451ed5e7c8a716696ea6a053b60b40bee9f65/lib/taskcompendium/src/taskcompendium/importers/harbor/package.py#L327-L355): separate grading and collect hooks.
- [Release task 002](https://github.com/OpenMOSS/SWE-bench-Science/blob/main/huggingface/tasks/task_002/pre_artifacts.sh): patch collection contract.

# Proposed Fix

1. Build on #11664 after it lands. Pin `OpenMOSS-Team/SWE-bench-Science@997408298e8e4d09978b1120b95c4540d1a71bcb`; read its selection manifest and require exactly the 96 unrestricted task IDs. Check the pinned snapshot's layout and image references before importing.
2. Extend package staging for the nested task directory and schema 1.3. Preserve each original `instruction.md`, timeout, CPU, memory, storage, and image digest. Run the release's patch-collection hook after mini-swe-agent exits, transfer `model.patch` to a fresh digest-pinned verifier machine, and keep private tests there.
3. Register a `swebench-science` catalog key and image lock using the existing mini-swe-agent protocol. Add it to the agentic suite after the smoke confirms that the selected resource and concurrency settings work.
4. Test selection, schema parsing, patch handoff, and verifier reward collection with small synthetic packages. Run the upstream no-model verifier smoke, then a served mini-swe-agent smoke and a full 96-task run; compare a sample patch's score with the upstream runner.
5. Publish the source pin, selected IDs, harness revision, environment and verifier digests, resource limits, concurrency, per-task scoring coverage, failure classes, and aggregate Pass@1 with the run artifacts. Complete the entry when all 96 tasks have a verifier result or a reported infrastructure failure.

comments.author: gonzalobenegas
comments.body:
🤖 On the 100 graded Qwen3.8-27B tasks, Pi 0.87.0 solved 3 and the authors’ Claude Code run solved 31 on the same IDs. All three Pi solves were also solved upstream. These 100 are the graded portion of an interrupted run.

I classified the last recorded model request by its system prompt and finish reason. In **75/100** trajectories, the last request was a compaction summary that reached its output limit. Of those, 74 ended at exactly 6,553 completion tokens and one at 4,096. This includes **21 of the 28** tasks solved only by the authors. It establishes a recurring failure mode. The number of solves recoverable by changing the limits is still open. [Authors’ per-task grades](https://github.com/swescience/swescience.github.io/blob/f16153e5c47c46b2f6f2ebf0aaefae34bdf8c8bd/data/task-matrix.json)

Pi budgets a main summary at 80% of the reserved output tokens, rounded down, and a split-turn prefix at 50%. With an 8,192-token reserve those limits are 6,553 and 4,096. Pi rejects a summary whose provider stop reason is length, including summaries containing partial text. The older Harbor investigation found a separate Terminus-2 fallback that could omit the latest tool observation. Its larger-budget follow-up also showed why completed handoffs, resumed solver steps and grades should be measured separately. [Pi 0.87.0 compaction implementation](https://unpkg.com/@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent@0.87.0/dist/core/compaction/compaction.js) · [Harbor #165](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/issues/165)

Two matched controls use tasks 012 and 015 at 65,536 context with explicit xhigh, at 8,192 and 16,384 reply tokens. Both tasks have public successful reference traces. The authors report 40,670 output tokens across 21 calls on 012 and 420,892 across 60 calls on 015. Their published aggregates do not give a per-call maximum. [Task 012](https://github.com/swescience/swescience.github.io/blob/f16153e5c47c46b2f6f2ebf0aaefae34bdf8c8bd/public/traces/qwen3-8-27b-xhigh/task-012.json) · [Task 015](https://github.com/swescience/swescience.github.io/blob/f16153e5c47c46b2f6f2ebf0aaefae34bdf8c8bd/public/traces/qwen3-8-27b-xhigh/task-015.json)

comments.author: gonzalobenegas
comments.body:
🤖 All four matched Pi attempts graded. At a 65,536-token context, doubling the per-reply limit recovered the authors’ task 012 solve. Task 015 still failed. This is one attempt per condition on two selected disagreements.

| Task | 32,768 context / 8,192 reply | 65,536 / 8,192 | 65,536 / 16,384 | Authors’ Claude Code |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 012 private tests | 5/10 | 5/10 | **10/10** | 10/10 |
| 015 private tests | 17/31 | 17/31 | 17/31 | 31/31 |

All four new attempts passed their public test. The checkpoint, Pi 0.87.0, xhigh, tasks and verifiers were held fixed. Both model-request receipts confirmed the intended reply cap and enabled thinking.

**012.** Neither 65,536-context attempt compacted. After normalizing generated tool-call IDs, the archived input messages matched on calls 1 through 9. On call 9 both had 19,407 prompt tokens. At the smaller cap the model used 8,192 tokens and returned no visible text or tool call. At the larger cap it used 15,364 tokens, requested two tools, and issued two edits on the next call. The native grade rose from zero to one. [Authors’ task 012 trace](https://github.com/swescience/swescience.github.io/blob/f16153e5c47c46b2f6f2ebf0aaefae34bdf8c8bd/public/traces/qwen3-8-27b-xhigh/task-012.json)

**015.** Increasing the reply limit also increased Pi’s compaction reserve, which changed when it summarized and how much recent history it kept. At the smaller cap, one of five summary calls finished normally. At the larger cap, four of nine did and coding resumed after each. The final summary still hit its limit of 13,107 tokens. Summaries used 90,981 of the 167,081 generated tokens in the larger-budget trace (54%). Passing more handoffs did not improve the native grade. The authors report 420,892 generated tokens across 60 calls on this task. [Authors’ task 015 trace](https://github.com/swescience/swescience.github.io/blob/f16153e5c47c46b2f6f2ebf0aaefae34bdf8c8bd/public/traces/qwen3-8-27b-xhigh/task-015.json)

**Frozen-summary replay on 015.** I replayed the final 21,393-token input on the same checkpoint at xhigh, with a fixed seed (42) shared across two output caps. Both replies stopped normally after 11,351 output tokens, at caps of 13,107 and 26,214. Both produced visible text with goal, progress, next steps and critical context headings. The archived live call had hit the 13,107 cap. This single replay shows that this input can finish within the existing limit and that another sample can behave differently. It did not resume the solver or produce a task grade. No content-quality score was assigned to the summaries.

spillover_issues.body:
## Summary

- **Motivation**
  - Both 10/05 Snowball SFT (`20.35%`) and Mochi Hero SFT (`20.43%`) used ~20% pretraining replay without testing other shares.
  - This sweep chooses the pretraining-replay share for Mochi SFT.

- **Goal**
  - Find the best pretraining-replay share (`0%` to `60%`) at a fixed number of drawn rows.

- **Data & Setup**
  - Long-loop SFT mix: `216` SFT stores (`184` sources) + `193` pretraining-replay sources.
  - Each arm varies only the replay share; internal proportions stay fixed.
  - Evaluations:
    - Held-out loss on `15` fixed sets: `4` pretraining-replay validation sets (`c13q3`, `c28q4`, `c30q4`, `c32q3`) + `11` disjoint SFT carve-outs (`agenttrove`, `identity-data`, and `nemotron_sft_v3` slices).
    - Snowball capabilities: [edit-call](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11536) (`1,197` items) + 14-clean-source Micro210 (two inference repeats).
    - Mochi capabilities: [edit-call](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11536) + 13-benchmark launcher suite (`--limit 100`).

- **Key Results**
  - **Pretraining loss is flat across `0%–60%` replay**
    - 1h Muon-H: `0.8549 → 0.8531` (base `0.8561`).
    - 8h Muon-H: `0.8523 → 0.8506`; Adam banks: `0.860–0.862`.
    - No run shows rising replay loss up to 500 updates.
  - **High replay (`40%–60%`) and `0%` replay hurt SFT loss and capabilities**
    - 1h Muon-H Micro210: **`32.86%`** at `10%` vs `27.08%` (`20.47%`), `25.77%` (`5%`), `25.35%` (`40%`), `24.04%` (`60%`).
    - 8h Muon-H: `10%` scored `48.58%` Micro210 and `0.5348` SFT loss vs `45.18%` / `0.5413` (`20.47%`) and `0.5913` (`40%`).
  - **With Adam expert banks (#11858), `10%` beats `0%` and gets the lowest 8h SFT loss**
    - 1h Micro210: **`54.69%`** (`10%`, P1) vs `52.32%` (`0%`, r0) and `51.75%` (`20.47%`, Arm E r2).
    - 1h SFT loss: `0.5032` (`10%`) vs `0.591` (`0%`).
    - 8h (`10%`, P3, seed 0): lowest SFT loss (**`0.4247`**) and `51.60%` Micro210 (`+6.42 pp` vs Muon-H control, `+1.04 pp` vs seed-2 `20.47%` P2, `-6.10 pp` vs seed-0 `20.47%` Arm E r2).
  - **Mochi continued from `step-400407` (`5%` vs `20.47%`, 8h `step-401600`)**
    - Edit-call: near ceiling and overlapping (`0.959/0.923` vs `0.947/0.932` vs baseline `0.918/0.931`).
    - Launcher: 9/10 usable evals within `0–4` points; **MRCR** dropped at `5%` (`23.46%` vs `30.40%`).
    - Confound: `step-400407` was already SFT'd with warm optimizer state.
  - **Mochi fresh from pre-trained base `step-393491` (`10%` replay + Adam banks, `128 GB200`)**
    - `step-100` (1h) → `step-1000` (8h, ~1/7th the updates of baseline `step-400407`):
      - Edit-call greedy exact: `0.526 → 0.673` (baseline `0.661`); reply length `599 → 268` tokens (baseline `250`).
      - 13-benchmark launcher: 10/13 rose; at or near baseline on `math500` (`93%` vs `94%`), `humanevalplus` (`84%` vs `85%`), `gsm8k` (`82%` vs `77%`), `truthfulqa` (`69.45%` vs `70.20%`).
      - Remaining gaps: `mmlu-pro` (`48%` vs `61–67%`), `mbppplus`, `triviaqa`, `ifbench`, `mrcr`.

- **Conclusion**
  - **`10%` pretraining replay** is the strongest share tested across both Muon-H and Adam-bank runs.
  - It avoids the SFT-loss and capability drops at `40%–60%` and `0%` while keeping pretraining loss flat.
  - On Mochi from pre-trained base (`step-393491`), `10%` replay + Adam banks trained stably to 1,000 updates on `128 GB200` and improved on edit-call and 10/13 launcher evals from `step-100` to `step-1000`, though a matched `20.47%` or Muon-H from-base control has not been run yet.
  - Most arms are single training runs; no causal claim is made.

Parent: #11535 · Related: #11858 (optimizer grid), #11687 (BF16 parameter storage fix).

🤖 **Reviewed edit-call results (all three one-hour replay arms): 63 of 855 (20.47%), 69 of 855 (40%), and 64 of 855 (60%).**

## Edit-call results

Each arm trains 150 updates (4,800 packed rows of 262,144 tokens) from the pre-train Snowball base on the same FP32 fallback control recipe (`6164fcbd`, routed expert banks on Muon-H; switched after the 2026-11-18 optimizer assignment hung on update 1, issue 11793), exported to BF16 and served once for this eval. The 20.47% arm is the 2026-11-19 from-base control run (same recipe, source, and seed, run at a different time). The eval covers 11 tasks and 58 files (171 prompts per pass; 855 pooled across seeds 1–5; exact match after stripping trailing whitespace).

| Arm | Seed 0 (of 171) | Greedy (of 171) | Seeds 1–5 | Pooled seeds 1–5 (of 855) | Strict calls (of 855 / 171 / 171) | Applied edits (of 855 / 171 / 171) |
|---|---:|---:|---|---:|---|---|
| 20.47% replay (2026-11-19 control) | 15 | 14 | 8, 14, 14, 13, 14 | 63 (.074; .045–.099) | 485 / 104 / 115 | 398 / 91 / 111 |
| **40% replay** | **14** | **19** | **10, 18, 15, 13, 13** | **69 (.081; .055–.113)** | **616 / 127 / 145** | **518 / 107 / 137** |
| **60% replay** | **12** | **18** | **15, 13, 10, 12, 14** | **64 (.075; .047–.101)** | **629 / 127 / 146** | **524 / 105 / 139** |

- **40% vs 20.47% pooled exact matches:** +6 (+0.70 pp), with 6 tasks up, 1 down, and 4 tied (per-task changes from −4 to +4).
- **60% vs 20.47% pooled exact matches:** +1 (+0.12 pp), with 4 tasks up, 4 down, and 3 tied (per-task changes from −2 to +3).
- **40% vs 60% pooled exact matches:** +5 (+0.58 pp), with 5 tasks up, 2 down, and 4 tied (per-task changes from −2 to +3). All intervals are a descriptive 95% bootstrap over the 11 tasks and overlap across all three arms.
- **Strict calls and applied edits vs exact matches:** both higher-replay arms emitted more strict edit calls (616 for 40% and 629 for 60%, against 485 for 20.47% pooled) and more applied edits (518 and 524, against 398), while exact matches stayed close (69 and 64, against 63); most of the extra applied edits differed from the target file (449 of 855 pooled for 40% and 460 of 855 for 60%, against 335 of 855 for 20.47%).

## Caveats

- **Base-stream exposure (at its real size):** base-stream exposure is unverified for every arm. Across the first 4,800 rows, the 40% arm drew 1,855 pretraining replay rows (38.65% of rows; 40.65% of trained tokens, about 2× the 20.47% arm's 954 rows) and the 60% arm drew 2,826 replay rows (58.88% of rows; 60.77% of trained tokens, about 3× the 20.47% arm's 954 rows, which were 19.88% of rows / 21.15% of trained tokens), so the unverified base-stream exposure caveat scales accordingly.
- **One run per arm and weak baseline recipe:** this compares one training run, one checkpoint export, and one serve per arm on a weak baseline recipe (the 2026-11-19 from-base control scored 87.29 of 440 on Micro210 against 145.01 for the 2026-11-18 control). With one training run per arm and overlapping task intervals, these three points do not establish a replay-share effect or optimum on edit calls.

**Correction (21 Nov):** the earlier version of this note listed data sources in sorted order, whereas `MixtureDataset` assigns dataset indices in the training config's `data.components` insertion order (Snowball's config order is not sorted; Mochi's runtime payload order is sorted, so all six Mochi rows are unchanged). Old → new for Snowball: pretrain replay 1 h `514 / 1,008 / 1,974 / 2,945` → `452 / 954 / 1,855 / 2,826` and 8 h `3,326 / 6,508` → `3,188 / 6,305`; identity draws 1 h `1 / 1 / 0 / 1` → `1 / 3 / 1 / 0` and 8 h `3 / 2` → `5 / 2` (1 h range `0 or 1` → `0 to 3`); zero-draw SFT sources (of 184) 1 h `61 / 69 / 80 / 93` → `61 / 69 / 78 / 82` (overall 1 h `61-93` → `61-91`: Snowball `61-82`, Mochi `88-91`) and 8 h `30 / 33` → `28 / 36`; the same-map sequence order holds across both Snowball recipes (18 Nov and 19 Nov), not between Snowball and Mochi.

Training data is drawn in blocks of 64,000 packed sequences (262,144 tokens each). Each source gets an exact slot count per block, its weight × 64,000. Within a block the slots are shuffled once, with the data seed. A run reads the block from position 0.
- A Snowball one-hour arm reads 150 × 32 = 4,800 sequences, 7.5% of one block. An 8-hour arm reads 500 × 32 = 16,000 (25%).
- A Mochi one-hour arm reads 143 × 16 = 2,288 (3.6%). The 8-hour plan reads 1,193 × 16 = 19,088 (29.8%).
- All arms use seed 0. Arms with the same map read the same sequence order on both Snowball recipes, so those same-map Snowball arms are not independent samples of the mix.   - pretrain replay is `pretrain/*`;

- **How it was reproduced:**
  - It runs Levanter's own `MixtureDataset` (`lib/levanter/src/levanter/data/mixture.py`, identical at Snowball pin 2d3a1574 and Mochi PR head 4540eedb) with placeholder datasets.
  - It uses each run's consumed `data.train_weights` (from the W&B config for Snowball and the frozen plan maps for Mochi), each run's submitted config component order (insertion order, which `MixtureDataset` keeps), block size 64,000 and the key `mix_key = split(split(PRNGKey(0), 2)[0])[0]`.
  - It reads `_get_block(0)` and decodes each slot id as `id >> 16`, the dataset index.
- **Self-check:** for every arm, the per-source counts over the full 64,000-slot block equal each source's slot count exactly. The script asserts this before counting.
- **Status:** reproduced with the loader's own code; the key path, component order, block assignment and batch-to-position mapping were checked against the pinned source. Pretrain-replay row counts match an independent count through the training data path (954 / 1,855 / 2,826 of 4,800); the runs log no per-source draws.
- **Mochi seed:** `trainer.seed` 0, `data_seed` None and `mixture_start_step` 400407 are read from each arm's frozen worker payload.
- **Packing:** packing differs between the Snowball and Mochi pins, so the counts are per source, not token-equal across stacks.

Both checkpoints are step 150, BF16-stored (`c150-base-replay10-1118eager` with 10% replay vs `c150-base-control-eager-20261118` with 20.47% replay).

### Headline (all 20 sources; harbor sources were scored)

| Run | Cluster | Native equal-20 | Pooled available | Score mass (of 440) | Excluded trials |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| run 49536 (10% r1) | `cw-rno2a` | 43.57% | 36.18% | 157.73 | 4 |
| run 49537 (10% r2) | `cw-rno2a` | 38.69% | 33.56% | 146.97 | 2 |
| run 44646 (20.47% control r1) | `cw-us-east-02a` | 39.18% | 32.29% | 141.76 | 1 |
| run 44647 (20.47% control r2) | `cw-us-east-02a` | 39.33% | 33.77% | 148.26 | 1 |

- **Mean mass:** 10% replay 152.35 vs 20.47% control 145.01 (**+7.35**). Repeat spread: 10% arm 10.76, control 6.50. Run 49537 (146.97) sits inside the control's range (141.76 to 148.26), so the repeats do not separate the 10% arm from the 20.47% control.
- **Native equal-20 mean:** 10% replay 41.13% vs 20.47% control 39.26% (**+1.87 pp**). Repeat spread: 10% arm 4.88 pp, control 0.15 pp. The gap is inside the 10% arm's own repeat spread.
- **Excluded trials** count as 0 in `avg_score` and mass. Arithmetic bounds (each excluded trial set to 0 or 1; not confidence intervals): run 49536 157.73 to 161.73, run 49537 146.97 to 148.97, run 44646 141.76 to 142.76, run 44647 148.26 to 149.26. All 6 arm and 2 control excluded trials are in harbor sources (10% arm: `bixbench-pi` 2, `swebench-verified` 1, `tb2-recovery` 1 in r1 and 2 in r2; 20.47% control: `ds-1000-local` 1, `tb2-recovery` 1).

### 14 clean sources and six harbor sources

| Arm (cluster) | 14-source mass r1 / r2 (mean) | Equal-weight 14 r1 / r2 (mean) | Six harbor sources mass r1 / r2 (mean) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|

- Repeat spreads: 14-source mass 10% arm 5.97, control 7.00; equal-weight 14 10% arm 2.97 pp, control 0.81 pp. The 14-source mass gain (+9.50) is larger than each arm's own mass spread, and the equal-weight gap (+4.38 pp) exceeds both spreads. The six harbor sources are noisy (a handful of tasks each) and their mass is lower in the 10% arm by 2.15.

### Per-source difference (mass, 10% mean minus 20.47% control mean)

- **Up:** MMLU-Pro +3.00, OlympiadBench +2.50, HumanEval+ +1.50, NUPA +1.50, GPQA +1.00, MBPP+ +1.00, swebench-verified +1.00, and six sources at +0.50.

- **40% vs 20.47% at 8 hours:** 40% is lower than 20.47% on all 10 rows (greedy applies `−0.029`; pooled applies `−0.050`; pooled strict `−0.056`).

- **Held-out SFT changes sign with the seed.** At seed 0, 10% was higher than 20.47% (+0.0337). At seed 2, 10% is lower (−0.0094).
- **Most of the seed-0 gap was identity-data** (+0.4167). Identity-data has 8 held-out sequences. At seed 0 the 10% run drew 1 identity sequence in training and the control drew 3. At seed 2 both runs drew 2.
- **Without identity-data, 10% is lower at both seeds:** −0.0069 at seed 0 and −0.0041 at seed 2 on the SFT source macro. Nemotron macro is also lower at 10% at both seeds.
- **Replay pretrain loss is slightly higher at 10% at both seeds** (+0.0010 and +0.0004).
- **Seed against seed:** the 10% runs differ by 0.0425 on held-out SFT (seed 2 lower), and almost all of that is identity-data. The 20.47% runs differ by 0.0007, but that pair also differs by training cluster.

## Limits

- Two seeds only. The seed-0 pair also differs by training cluster, so the seed and cluster effects cannot be separated there.
- These are held-out losses only. No capability eval has been run on the seed-2 models.
- These numbers do not show what caused any difference.

**Edit-call eval (eval-r2, step 150) of 10% vs 20.47% replay on the 18 Nov recipe (18 Nov baseline: expert banks on Adam, norm scales on Muon-H; see issue 11858), at trainer seed 2 beside the original seed-0 runs.** Seed 2: both models trained and scored on `cw-rno2a`. Seed 0: both scored on `cw-us-east-02a` (the 20.47% run trained on `cw-us-east-02a`, the 10% run on `cw-rno2a`). Each cell is a single training run and a single eval serve.

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

Δ = 10% − 20.47% within a seed. Intervals are 95% file-level bootstrap intervals.

## What the table shows

- **Within each seed:** 10% is below 20.47% at both seeds on call, parses, strict and applies, greedy and pooled. The seed-2 gaps are larger on call and parses (pooled −0.100 at seed 2, −0.008 at seed 0).
- **Intervals:** at seed 2, the pooled call and parses intervals do not overlap; all other seed-2 intervals overlap.
- **exact_ts:** the sign differs between seeds (seed 2: +0.052 greedy, +0.035 pooled; seed 0: −0.059 greedy, −0.012 pooled).
- **Seed to seed:** the seed-2 models score higher than the seed-0 models on 17 of 20 model-rate pairs, equal on 1 and lower on 2, all on exact_ts (for example, 20.47% pooled call 0.896 vs 0.764). Seed and scoring cluster are not separated in this difference: the seed-2 pair was scored on `cw-rno2a` and the seed-0 pair on `cw-us-east-02a`.

## Setup and scope

- **Training:** one run per cell, 150 updates on the 18 Nov recipe. Within a seed, the replay share is the only intended difference. The seed-2 runs differ from the seed-0 runs in trainer seed (0 → 2).
- **Scoring:** the same eval code, prompt assignment (`81b24364ef20`), verifier and scorer for all four cells. 1197/1197 rows each, with 0 unexpected, 0 duplicated and 0 errors.
- **Single runs:** these are single-run differences, not established effects.

🤖 **Micro210, 19 Nov / 6164 recipe, one-hour: 10% vs 20.47% replay**

All models are one-hour runs at step 150, FP32-stored, trained and scored on cw-us-east-02a with the same protocol. The 10% model was FP32-trained and downcast to BF16 for export; that downcast is attested by the selection chain only. Each model has two scoring repeats; they are two inference runs of one training run each, so the repeats do not measure training-seed variance.

## Headline: the 14 clean sources (equal weight)
| | Equal-weight 14, repeat 1 / repeat 2 (mean, spread) | 14-source mass of 340, repeat 1 / repeat 2 (mean, spread) |
|---|---|---|
| 10% replay | 35.23% / 30.49% (32.86%, 4.74 pp) | 92.45 / 103.79 (98.12, 11.34) |
| 20.47% replay (control) | 29.26% / 24.89% (27.08%, 4.37 pp) | 86.30 / 86.28 (86.29, 0.01) |
| 10% minus 20.47% | +5.78 pp | +11.83 |

The equal-weight gap (+5.78 pp) is above both repeat spreads (4.74 and 4.37 pp), and the repeats do not overlap: the 10% lower repeat (30.49%) is 1.23 pp above the 20.47% upper repeat (29.26%). In mass both 10% repeats (92.45, 103.79) sit above both 20.47% repeats (86.30, 86.28), by 6.15 and 17.49 (against the upper control repeat, 86.30). The mass gap (+11.83) is about equal to the 10% spread (11.34).

## Per-source mass, 10% minus 20.47% (14 clean sources, mean of repeats)
Up: AIME24 +5.00, MMLU-Pro +2.00, TruthfulQA +2.00, GSM8K +1.50, HumanEval+ +1.50, OlympiadBench +1.00, MBPP+ +1.00, IFBench +1.00, MATH-500 +0.50. Down: GPQA -2.50, TriviaQA -1.00, MRCR -0.17. Flat: NUPA, CruxEval. AIME24 and OlympiadBench have 100 sequences each (200 of the 340 clean sequences), so they weigh heavily in mass; in the equal-weight view each source counts 1/14.

## The 19 Nov replay curve (14 clean sources only)
All one-hour, step 150, trained and scored on cw-us-east-02a, one training run per share, two scoring repeats each.

Differences from the 20.47% control, equal-weight / mass: 10% +5.78 pp / +11.83; 40% -1.73 pp / -6.55; 60% -3.04 pp / -16.47. The 40% and 60% rows come from the earlier Micro210 notes.

## All 20 sources for the 10% pair (secondary; Harbor prepare failures are comparable here)
| Run | Native equal-20 | Pooled available | Score mass (of 440) | Excluded Harbor trials |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 10% repeat 1 | 24.66% | 21.06% | 92.45 | 1 |
| 10% repeat 2 | 21.68% | 24.10% | 105.79 | 1 |
| 20.47% repeat 1 | 20.65% | 19.89% | 87.30 | 1 |
| 20.47% repeat 2 | 17.59% | 19.84% | 87.28 | 0 |

Means: native equal-20 23.17% against 19.12% (+4.05 pp; spreads 2.98 and 3.06 pp); mass 99.12 against 87.29 (+11.83). Harbor trials scored of 100: 10% 99 and 99; 20.47% 99 and 100.

## Answer length (total response tokens over total sequences, 14 clean sources)
10%: 7,755 and 7,534; 20.47%: 7,149 and 7,379. Length stops of 340: 124 and 118 against 121 and 122.

- One training run per share. The models differ in replay share; the 10% model also passed through a BF16 downcast for export. These numbers do not show what caused any difference.

## Micro210, 6164 recipe, 8-hour (500 updates): 10% replay beside the 20.47% and 40% rows

Third 8-hour point for the replay-share question. **The 10% run was trained and scored on cw-rno2a. The 20.47% and 40% runs were trained and scored on cw-us-east-02a.** Same protocol, step 500, two scoring repeats per model (two inference runs of one training run each, so the repeats do not measure training-seed variance). The 10% model is a BF16 export; I do not state its training precision beyond that. The 20.47% and 40% rows are from the earlier 8-hour 40% vs 20.47% comment on this issue.

**Besides the replay share, the 10% run differs from the other two in three ways** (from a diff of each run's consumed training config): the training cluster (cw-rno2a, not cw-us-east-02a); the source commit, whose code adds a 1,800 s post-rebind barrier at the first step that the other two runs did not have; and the task timeout (50,400 s, not 31,800 s). The other differing keys are run names and output paths. A same-cluster 8-hour 20.47% control on cw-rno2a is being prepared.

## Headline: the 14 clean sources (equal weight)
| | Equal-weight 14, repeat 1 / repeat 2 (mean, spread) | 14-source mass of 340, repeat 1 / repeat 2 (mean, spread) |

🤖

## Mochi launcher results: baseline, 20% replay and 5% replay on 13 evaluations

Three Mochi models, scored with the evaluation launcher from PR 11528 (head `b3611d8a`): the sealed step-400407 baseline, and the 20% and 5% replay models (8-hour arms, step 401600). Each model ran on its own vLLM server (16 GB200 GPUs, data parallel 16). These are launcher rows. Compare Mochi only with Mochi on this launcher.

## Row rules
- `--limit 100`: the first 100 source items of each evaluation (AIME24: 30 problems x 10 trials = 300 samples; GPQA-Diamond: 100 questions x 3 trials = 300). One trial per item elsewhere.
- Reply cap 16,384 tokens, 32 concurrent requests per evaluator, one evaluator at a time. Thinking on for AIME24, GPQA-Diamond, MMLU-Pro and MATH-500; off for the other nine.
- **A reply cut at its cap counts as wrong**, whatever letter or answer the grader extracted. The cap is 16,384 tokens, except CRUXEval (2,048) and NUPA5K-loose (256), whose tasks set their own. Unscored items would also count as wrong; none are unscored here.
- The launcher's own score is shown beside the capped score where they differ. It credits answers extracted from cut-off replies.
- Flags: 10% or more of replies cut at the cap means "cap-bound" and the row is not used to rank. If two models' cut shares differ by 5 points or more, the row is "cap-affected".

## Results (capped score; launcher score in brackets where different)

| Evaluation (items) | Baseline | 20% | 5% | Cut at cap (baseline / 20% / 5%) | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| AIME24 (300) | 63.00% (64.33%) | 63.67% (64.67%) | 62.00% (63.33%) | 108 / 105 / 110 | cap-bound, unranked |
| GPQA-Diamond (300) | 57.67% (72.00%) | 61.67% (73.67%) | 58.67% (70.33%) | 108 / 104 / 108 | cap-bound, unranked |
| MMLU-Pro (100) | 61.00% | 67.00% | 63.00% (65.00%) | 3 / 2 / 4 | usable |
| MATH-500 (100) | 94.00% | 96.00% | 96.00% | 4 / 3 / 1 | usable |
| GSM8K 0-shot, flexible-extract (100) | 77.00% | 79.00% | 82.00% | 0 / 0 / 0 | usable (strict-match is 0.00% for all three: its pattern never matches these replies) |
| TriviaQA, extract_answer (100) | 73.00% | 65.00% | 66.00% | 0 / 0 / 0 | usable |
| TruthfulQA, acc (100) | 70.20% | 70.62% | 70.35% | 0 / 0 / 0 | usable |
| HumanEval+ (100) | 85.00% | 89.00% | 90.00% | 0 / 0 / 0 | usable |
| MBPP+ (100) | 82.00% | 77.00% | 78.00% | 0 / 0 / 0 | usable |
| CRUXEval (100) | 90.00% | 87.00% | 84.00% (85.00%) | 2 / 4 / 3 | usable |
| IFBench, strict prompt (100) | 37.00% | 36.00% | 35.00% | 0 / 0 / 0 | usable |
| MRCR, accuracy (100) | 28.27% | 30.40% | 23.46% | 0 / 0 / 0 | usable |
| NUPA5K-loose, exact match (100) | 15.00% | 12.00% | 16.00% | 48 / 51 / 54 | cap-bound at its 256-token task cap, cap-affected, unranked |

Among the replies that were not cut, AIME24 is correct on 98.44% / 97.95% / 97.89% (baseline / 20% / 5%) and GPQA-Diamond on 90.10% / 94.39% / 91.67%. On GPQA-Diamond the launcher's own score credits 43 / 36 / 35 cut replies, which is why it is far above the capped score.

## Notes
- **Code evaluations.** In the first full runs, HumanEval+, MBPP+ and CRUXEval could not be graded on this branch: the grader's setup step ran before the answer file was installed (fixed on `main` by `1a8a628d26`, PR 11408). The three code rows come from reruns with that commit cherry-picked onto the PR head; the replies are fresh samples, not re-grades. All other rows come from the first runs on the PR head alone.
- **Replaced baseline run.** The first baseline rerun of the code evaluations was replaced: its server failed to start, so it was cancelled and launched again.
- **Transient errors.** A few single requests hit a connection error at the model call (MMLU-Pro once per model; also single items in GSM8K, TriviaQA and NUPA5K-loose in some runs). Each recovered on its first retry, and every item is scored in every row.

## What this does not show
- Each usable row is 100 items, one trial per item, one run per model, with no seed replicate (AIME24 and GPQA-Diamond run 10 and 3 trials per item, and are unranked). Differences of a few points are inside what one run of this size can resolve.
- AIME24, GPQA-Diamond and NUPA5K-loose are unranked, because 35 to 54% of replies hit their cap.
- It does not show why any model differs from another: nothing here separates training changes from sampling noise.

## Reading
On the usable rows the 20% and 5% models are mostly within a few points of each other (the largest gaps are MRCR, 30.40% vs 23.46%, and MMLU-Pro, 67% vs 63%), within what a single n=100 run resolves. Against the baseline, both 8-hour models score lower on TriviaQA (65% and 66% vs 73%), MBPP+ (77% and 78% vs 82%) and CRUXEval (87% and 84% vs 90%), and higher on HumanEval+ (89% and 90% vs 85%).

## Result

At one hour (150 updates, step 150, trainer seed 0), we compare three runs with expert banks on Adam, all trained and scored on cw-rno2a, that differ in the pretraining replay share: **r0** (0% replay), **P1** (10% replay) and the one-hour **arm E r2** (20.47% replay). The bank-optimizer results for P1 and arm E r2 are in issue 11858 (https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11858#issuecomment-7095004990).

- **Held-out loss:** r0's SFT loss is higher than both (0.5912 vs 0.5032 for P1 and 0.5016 for arm E r2). The identity-data set is much higher (2.3100 vs 1.2696 and 1.1933), while the Nemotron SFT v3 macro and agenttrove losses are slightly lower. On the pooled SFT loss, r0 is about equal (0.2228 vs 0.2255 and 0.2229). Its pretrain macro loss is slightly higher (0.8618 vs 0.8597 and 0.8578).
- **Edit-call:** The r0 and P1 intervals overlap for every reported rate (pooled applied edits 0.806 vs 0.774). r0 is higher than arm E r2 on every tool-call, parse, strict-format and applied-edit rate, with non-overlapping intervals (pooled applied edits 0.806 vs 0.642).

All reported edit-call intervals overlapped, and r0 averaged 2.37 percentage points lower on equal-weight Micro210. Across the three replay shares, the Micro210 means are not monotonic (52.32%, 54.69%, 51.75%), so we claim no replay trend. Arm E r2 was trained on a different code commit, so gaps against it combine the replay share and the code. One training run per model.

- Replies with no edit call, meaning the scorer found no edit call in either the server-parsed output or the reply text (greedy / pooled): P3 18 / 117, arm E r2 17 / 83, P2 10 / 72, plain 10% 14 / 91. Of P3's, 37 have JSON inside `<tool_call>` that parses once one or two closing braces are added, against 2 for arm E r2.

## Micro210

Two inference repeats of one checkpoint each, all scored on cw-rno2a.

| 14 clean sources | equal-weight mean, repeat 1 / repeat 2 (mean, spread) | mass of 340, repeat 1 / repeat 2 (mean, spread) |
|---|---|---|
| P3 (10%) | 51.02% / 52.18% (51.60%, 1.16 pp) | 140.16 / 134.35 (137.26, 5.81) |
| arm E r2 (20.47%) | 56.66% / 58.73% (57.70%, 2.07 pp) | 148.72 / 154.29 (151.51, 5.57) |
| P2 (20.47%, seed 2) | 52.01% / 49.11% (50.56%, 2.90 pp) | 138.39 / 138.35 (138.37, 0.03) |
| plain 10% | 50.31% / 46.84% (48.58%, 3.47 pp) | 139.37 / 128.45 (133.91, 10.92) |
| P3 − arm E r2 | −6.10 pp | −14.25 |
| P3 − P2 | +1.04 pp | −1.11 |

- **Against arm E r2:** the highest P3 repeat is 4.48 pp below the lowest arm E r2 repeat on equal weight, and 8.56 below it on mass.
- **Against P2:** the ranges overlap on both views.
- **Where the mass gap sits (P3 − arm E r2):** AIME24 −4.00, IFBench −3.00, GPQA −2.50, CRUXEval −1.50; MMLU-Pro +1.00.
- **All 20 sources:** P3 41.43%, arm E r2 45.83% (−4.40 pp); P3's excluded Harbor trials (4 and 1) are among the larger ones.

## Limits

- One seed-0 arm E training run at each replay share. The edit-call intervals cover file-level sampling only, and the two Micro210 repeats cover inference only; neither measures training-seed variation. The held-out losses have no interval.
- P2 differs from arm E r2 by seed (and data order), not replay; it is context for how far two arm E runs can sit apart, not a noise estimate.
- 8-hour rows on cw-rno2a only.

### B. Code evaluations (thinking off)

CRUXEval: 12 of 100 step-1000 replies hit the task cap (3 graded correct). Among the 88 replies that were not cut, 85.23% were correct, against 86.60 to 91.84% for the comparators.

### Run notes
- The step-1000 orchestrator was restarted once after its first serve and evaluation child were killed. A replacement serve loaded 16 of 16 engines. Five evaluation children were preempted and resumed from saved records: AIME24, GPQA-Diamond and MMLU-Pro once each, MATH-500 five times and CRUXEval three times.

MMLU-Pro, GSM8K, TriviaQA and TruthfulQA also have 1, 1, 1 and 2 finished `APIConnectionError` rows, each recovered on retry 1. No evaluation has unscored items, an unrecovered infrastructure error or a deadline hit.

n = 100 items per evaluation, one run per model, one training run per configuration. ## Summary

- **Motivation**
  - Long-loop rounds dropped from Exp1 (SFT 746 → RL 16: Micro `0.4526` / mean `0.5216`) to Exp2 (`0.4048 / 0.4829`) and Exp4 (`0.3763 / 0.4250`; #11337) while several SFT settings changed together.
  - Isolating which SFT knob drove the drop directly guides the Mochi SFT recipe.

- **Goal**
  - Identify which Exp1-to-Exp4 SFT setting change(s) account for lower general and agentic ability.

- **Data & Setup**
  - Base model: Snowball pre-trained base (`snowball-67b-a2b-base-262k-qk175-skew8`), fresh SFT, FP32-stored parameters (except Arm C).
  - Two SFT mixes:
    - **18 Nov mix:** used only for the initial LR and grad-clip screens.
    - **19 Nov / 6164 mix** (`20.47%` replay baseline, or `10%` in P1/P3): used for all other 1-hour and 8-hour arms.
  - Method: change one knob at a time at 1 hour (`150` updates), then validate decisive arms at 8 hours (`500` updates) on held-out loss, [edit-call](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11536) (`1,197` items), and 14-clean-source Micro210 (two inference repeats).

- **Key Results (8-hour, step 500, 19 Nov / 6164 mix, `cw-rno2a`)**
  - **Expert banks on Adam — Arm E r2 (seed 0, `20.47%` replay) vs Muon-H control**
    - Held-out SFT loss: `0.4488` vs `0.5413`.
    - Micro210: **`57.70%`** vs `45.18%` (**`+12.52 pp`**).
    - Edit-call: intervals overlap (`0.825` vs `0.765` pooled applies). ([loss](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11858#issuecomment-7078520306), [edit-call](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11858#issuecomment-7080258692), [Micro210](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11858#issuecomment-7081822894))
  - **Seed replicate — P2 (Adam banks, seed 2, `20.47%` replay)**
    - Held-out SFT loss: `0.4425`.
    - Micro210: **`50.56%`** (`+5.38 pp` over control, `-7.13 pp` vs seed 0).
    - Edit-call: overlapping (`0.782`). ([details](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11858#issuecomment-7104658330))
  - **Adam banks + `10%` replay — P3 (seed 0)**
    - Lowest held-out SFT loss: **`0.4247`**.
    - Micro210: **`51.60%`** (`+6.42 pp` over control, `+1.04 pp` over P2, `-6.10 pp` vs seed-0 `20.47%`).
    - Edit-call: overlapping (`0.768`). ([details](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11858#issuecomment-7104658330))
  - **RMSProp-style expert banks — Arm F (2nd moment only, no momentum, seed 0)**
    - Held-out SFT loss: `0.4433` (similar to Adam banks).
    - Sampled edit-call: `0.674` (below Arm E and control, non-overlapping intervals).
    - Micro210: `50.51%` (`-7.19 pp` vs Arm E r2; repeats overlap control).
    - Short 20-step Mochi Bank-RMS probes also failed the stability rule (`1.715x` twin loss, grad norm `218.67`). ([8h Arm F](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11858#issuecomment-7087782018), [Mochi probes](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11858#issuecomment-7080948760))

- **Conclusion**
  - Routing **4-D MoE expert banks to Adam** (keeping Muon-H on attention and 2-D/3-D matrices) is the dominant SFT lever at both 1 hour (`+24.99 pp` Micro210) and 8 hours (`+5.38` to `+12.52 pp` Micro210, ~`0.10–0.12` lower SFT loss).
  - Dropping momentum (RMSProp-style banks) matches SFT loss but trails on capabilities.
  - One training run per configuration; no causal claim is made.

comments.body:
🤖 **Scale difference from Exp1–Exp4 and Arm 1 dependency**

## Scale comparison

Our one-at-a-time SFT ablations run at 1/8th the per-update batch size of Exp1–Exp4:

| Setting | Exp1–Exp4 runs | Our 64-H100 ablations |
|---|---|---|
| Hardware | 32 hosts × 8 H100 (256 H100 in Exp1) | 8 hosts × 8 H100 (64 H100; mesh `context=8`, `data=8`) |
| Packed rows per update | 256 (`256 × 262,144` = 67,108,864 tokens) | 32 (`trainer.trainer.train_batch_size: 32`; `32 × 262,144` = 8,388,608 tokens, 1/8×) |
| Microbatch / accumulation | — | `gradient_accumulation_steps: 4` (4 microbatches of 8 rows scanned inside one update; loss divided by the full 32-row scored-token count, `_accumulated_loss_and_grads` at commit `3b291b10`) |
| Updates per run (`stop_after_steps`) | 204 (Exp2), 360 (Exp4), 388 (Exp3), 746 (Exp1) | 150 (one-hour size); 500 (8-hour size) |
| Raw tokens per run | 13.69 B (204 updates) to 50.06 B (746 updates) | 1.26 B (150 updates, 4,800 rows); 4.19 B (500 updates, 16,000 rows) |

Because both batch size per update (8×) and total trained tokens are smaller than Exp1–Exp4, effects that depend on batch size or longer training horizons may differ between the one-hour screen, the 8-hour screen, and 256-H100 scale.

## Arm 1 dependency

Arm 1 (changing stored parameter precision from BF16 to FP32 under Exp1's optimizer routing, with 4-D routed expert banks on Adam and stacked norm scales on Muon-H) waits on issue 11793 (first-update hang under that combination on the current long-loop runtime). Isolating optimizer routing on FP32 likewise waits on issue 11793, while the BF16 single-knob arms and an FP32 combined precision-plus-routing check do not hit issue 11793.

## Research

This is a multi-run experiment with no results yet. The historical comparison also changes RL duration (16 versus 36 updates), so SFT-only scores cannot by themselves explain the post-RL gap. [#11687](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11687) documents the BF16 stored-parameter caveat in the Exp1-style baseline; [#11793](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11793) blocks the FP32 plus Exp1-routing comparison on the current runtime. The Exp3/Exp4 supervision sidecar is hash-pinned in [`exp3_recipe.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/1be0454367925411db6a432da3f62901881f8152/experiments/post_training/long_loop/exp3_recipe.py#L114-L126), but its per-source loss modes still need to be checked against the intended mask arm.

## Plan

1. Freeze the pre-train checkpoint, 10/05 catalog, source-loss sidecar and hash, runtime revision, data order, update count, and evaluation policy. Inspect the sidecar's per-source modes and verify that each arm changes only its named setting. Split the proposed LR/betas/eps and packing-cap/lookahead arms; separate expert-bank and norm routing if those assignments can be varied independently.
2. Run a matched Exp1-style BF16 baseline and one-hour SFT screens with the same source weights, sampling seed, update count, and checkpoint steps. Record consumed token counts because packing and masking change them. Score each checkpoint on the same frozen Micro210 and edit-call evaluations. Repeat the baseline to measure run and evaluation variation before promoting an arm whose score change exceeds that spread.
3. Keep the FP32 plus Exp1-routing cell gated on #11793. Once update 1 completes reliably, run a matched precision × routing comparison, then take only the decisive settings to eight-hour, repeated SFT runs. Report both Micro aggregates, benchmark-level scores, coverage, edit-call scores, seeds, configs, and checkpoint links, including negative results.
4. For any SFT setting that plausibly explains the gap, continue a matched pair through the same RL recipe and number of updates. Compare the post-RL checkpoints under one evaluation policy before attributing any part of the Exp1-to-Exp4 post-RL difference to SFT.

comments.author: karansag
comments.body:
🤖 **Optimizer routing per recipe: Exp1's expert banks fall through to Adam**

Source-verified parameter routing across five recipes (Exp1, Exp2, Exp3/Exp4 Hero-EP, the 11-19 control at `6164fcbd`, and the 10/05 run). No claim is made here about which routing performs better.

Conventions used below: `learning_rate` drives Muon-H and AdamH; `adam_lr` drives Adam. "Per-group" clip means `max_grad_norm` applied separately inside each optimizer group; "Global" means one gradient-norm clip across all parameters.

## Cross-recipe overview

| Weight group | Exp1 (`9662fdba02`, `bcf85728`) | Exp3 / Exp4 (`facbad18`) & 11-19 control (`6164fcbd`, `1f9bb1af`) | Real 10/05 (`ce7c77a`, `11baea1f`) | Exp2 (`442bf9d878`, `AdamConfig`) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Expert banks (`w_gate`, `w_up`, `w_down`)** | **Adam** (4-D fall-through) | Muon-H | Muon-H | Adam |
| Attention & shared-expert matrices | Muon-H | Muon-H | Muon-H | Adam |
| Gated norms | Muon-H | Muon-H | Muon-H | Adam |
| Stacked per-layer RMSNorm scales `(L, D)` | **Muon-H** (2-D match; no norm rule) | Adam | Adam | Adam |
| `embed_norm` / `final_norm` scales (1-D) | Adam | Adam | Adam | Adam |
| `output_proj` / LM head | AdamH | AdamH | AdamH | Adam |
| `token_embed`, `router`, `router_bias`, `attn_gate` | Adam | Adam | Adam | Adam |
| Clipping | none | global 1.0 | none | global 1.0 |

Every recipe except Exp2 uses mixed routing, with `token_embed`, `router`, `router_bias`, `attn_gate`, and `output_proj` routed the same way across all mixed recipes; Exp2 is the only recipe applying plain Adam uniformly to all parameters.

## Per-recipe routing tables (verified from source)

### (a) Exp1 (`9662fdba02`)

Optimizer `grug_moe_muonh_v1`, blob `bcf85728`; mask at `experiments/grug/moe/optimizer.py:285-307`. The SFT runtime stacks transformer blocks (`Transformer.stacked_blocks: ArrayStacked[Block]`, `sft_runtime/model.py:1251, 1283`), turning `(E, D, I)` expert weights (`levanter/grug/grug_moe.py:389-392`) into 4-D `(L, E, D, I)` leaves.

| Group | Optimizer | LR field | Clip |
|---|---|---|---|
| `token_embed`, `router`, `router_bias`, `attn_gate` | Adam (`L291-297`) | `adam_lr` `5e-5` | none |
| `output_proj` (LM head) | AdamH (`L298-299`) | `learning_rate` `5e-5` | none |
| gated norms (`embed`, `attn`, `mlp`, `final`) | Muon-H (`L301-302`) | `learning_rate` | none |
| attention `w_q/k/v/o`, shared expert `w_*`, latent `w_*` (stacked 3-D) | Muon-H (`L303-304`) | `learning_rate` | none |
| **expert banks `w_gate`/`w_up`/`w_down` (4-D)** | **Adam** (`L305` fall-through) | **`adam_lr`** | none |
| stacked RMSNorm scales `(L, D)` (2-D) | **Muon-H** (`L303-304`; no norm rule in this blob) | `learning_rate` | none |
| `embed_norm` and `final_norm` scales (1-D) | Adam (`L305`) | `adam_lr` | none |

`max_grad_norm: null` (`sft.yaml:75`) and blob `bcf85728` has no global clip option. Both `learning_rate` and `adam_lr` are `5e-5` (`sft.yaml:61, 73`), so the Adam fall-through changed the update rule for expert banks without changing their LR value.

### (b) Exp3 / Exp4 Hero-EP (blob `facbad18`)

Optimizer `grug_moe_hero_ep_muonh_v1`; mask at `moe_hero_ep/optimizer.py:308-327`.

| Group | Optimizer | LR field | Clip |
|---|---|---|---|
| `token_embed`, `router_bias`, `.attn_gate`, `.router` | Adam (`L314-315`) | `adam_lr = 5e-5 * 3/13 = 1.1538e-5` | global 1.0 |
| `output_proj` / `lm_head` | AdamH (`L316-317`) | `learning_rate` `5e-5` | global 1.0 |
| gated norms | Muon-H (`L319-320`) | `learning_rate` | global 1.0 |
| any `.weight` (RMSNorm scales, ShortConv) | Adam (`L323-324`) | `adam_lr` | global 1.0 |
| expert banks (4-D) and other 2/3-D matrices | Muon-H (`L325-326`; normalised per expert bank via `expert_normalization`, `L86-92`) | `learning_rate` | global 1.0 |

Per-group `max_grad_norm` is `None`. Global `1.0` clipping is set outside the optimizer (`global_gradient_clip=1`, `exp3_recipe:138`) and applied in `train_lm.py:328-329`.

### (c) 11-19 control (`6164fcbd`)

Optimizer `grug_moe_muonh_v1`, blob `1f9bb1af`; mask at `experiments/grug/moe/optimizer.py:339-363`.

| Group | Optimizer | LR field | Clip |
|---|---|---|---|
| `token_embed`, `router_bias`, `.attn_gate`, `.router` | Adam (`L345-351`) | `adam_lr` `2e-5` | global 1.0 |
| `output_proj` / `lm_head` | AdamH (`L352-353`) | `learning_rate` `2e-5` | global 1.0 |
| gated norms | Muon-H (`L355-356`) | `learning_rate` | global 1.0 |
| `.weight` (norm scales) | Adam (`L357-358`) | `adam_lr` | global 1.0 |
| 2/3/4-D matrices incl. expert banks | Muon-H (`L359-360`; 4-D banks use the hero backend with `expert_normalization: all_experts`, `use_syrk: true`, build `L263-297`) | `learning_rate` | global 1.0 |

Clipping comes from `global_grad_norm: 1.0` applied once before all groups (`L329-337`); per-group `max_grad_norm` is `null`. Routing matches Hero-EP `(b)`, and both use `expert_normalization: all_experts` and `use_syrk: true` (`moe_hero_ep/optimizer.py:228, 230` defaults in Exp3/Exp4); they differ in LRs (`learning_rate` `2e-5` vs `5e-5`; `adam_lr` `2e-5` vs `1.1538e-5`), with `1f9bb1af` sending 4-D leaves through the hero backend and 2/3-D leaves through the generic backend.

### (d) Real 10/05 run (`ce7c77a`, HF model card revision `8c76b22a`)

Trainer `experiments/grug_sft/special_token_lr.py` (`use_array_stacked_blocks=True` at `L334`); optimizer `experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/optimizer.py` `GrugMoeMuonHConfig` (blob `11baea1f`, not `bcf85728`).

| Group | Optimizer | LR field | Clip |
|---|---|---|---|
| `token_embed`, `router_bias`, `.attn_gate`, `.router` | Adam (`L306-312`) | `adam_lr` `5e-5` | none |
| `output_proj` / `lm_head` | AdamH (`L313-314`) | `learning_rate` `5e-5` | none |
| stacked `rms_attn` / `rms_mlp` scales | Adam (`L317-318`, `rmsnorm_to_adam=True`) | `adam_lr` | none |
| gated norms | Muon-H (`L320-321`) | `learning_rate` | none |
| 2/3/4-D matrices incl. **expert banks** | **Muon-H** (`L328-329`) | `learning_rate` | none |

Config sets `learning_rate=5e-5`, `adam_lr=5e-5`, `max_grad_norm=None` (`special_token_lr.py:361-373`) with no global clip. One extra rule scales updates to the 7 special-token rows of `token_embed` and `output_proj` by `×√32` after the optimizer (`special_token_train.py:498-505`).

### (e) Exp2 (`442bf9d878`)

Plain Levanter `AdamConfig` (`levanter/optim/config.py:503-535`) with a single group (no mask, no `multi_transform`): every parameter gets `clip_by_global_norm(1.0)`, then `scale_by_adam`, then `lr = 5e-5`. Weight decay is `0`, so the decay mask is unused.

## Evidence that Exp1's 4-D expert-bank fall-through was unintended

- **Docstring mismatch:** The same blob `bcf85728` lists `"MoE MLP"` under `muonh` (`experiments/grug/moe/optimizer.py:215`).
- **`(2, 3)` rule vs. stacked 4-D banks:** The `ndim in (2, 3)` rule was written for the `grug/moe` template (`grug/moe/model.py`, `blocks: tuple[Block, ...]`), where expert weights are 3-D and match Muon-H. `sft_runtime/model.py` stacks blocks into `ArrayStacked[Block]`, making expert banks 4-D, and the mask in `bcf85728` was not updated for 4-D leaves.
- **Explicit 10/05 comment:** The 10/05 optimizer (`experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/optimizer.py:322-327`, blob `11baea1f`) explicitly guards against this trap: *"plus 4D when use_array_stacked_blocks=True… Without including 4D, stacked expert weights fall through to adam"*.
- **Branch fix not in `main`:** Commit `02c96d8378` (2026-11-17, `"[grug] Preserve Muon state across expert routing"`, no commit message body) adds 4-D routing, the `.weight` → Adam rule, and `test_muonh_groups_match_hero_for_stacked_and_unstacked_models`. It is present in `6164fcbd` but **not in `main`**.
- **Still in `origin/main`:** `origin/main` (blob `81304114`, `L311`) still checks `ndim in (2, 3)`, so any stacked-block run on `main` using `grug_moe_muonh_v1` repeats Exp1's routing (which current recipes on `main` use it was not checked).
- Nothing found in source records the Exp1 fall-through routing as a deliberate choice.

## What Exp1 → Exp3 changed in optimizer routing

Moving from Exp1 (`bcf85728`) to Exp3 (`facbad18`) changed three optimizer behaviors together:

1. **Expert banks (`w_gate`/`w_up`/`w_down`):** Adam → Muon-H (with per-expert-bank `expert_normalization`).
2. **Stacked per-layer RMSNorm scales `(L, D)`:** Muon-H → Adam (via the `.weight` rule, and at `adam_lr = 1.1538e-5` instead of `5e-5`).
3. **Gradient clipping:** none → global norm clip `1.0` (`global_gradient_clip=1` in `exp3_recipe:138`, applied in `train_lm.py:328-329`).

## Unverified detail

How generic Muon (`_grug_scale_with_muon`) handles Exp1's stacked `(L, D)` RMSNorm scales was **not traced or verified**. As a 2-D leaf they may be orthogonalised across layers as a single matrix, so that behavior is left open rather than stated as fact.

## Open question for experiment owners

Was Adam on the 4-D expert banks (and Muon-H on stacked RMSNorm scales) in Exp1 intended, or an unintended result of stacking blocks under the `ndim in (2, 3)` rule?

comments.body:
🤖

## Held-out loss: LR 5e-5 with and without clipping (18 Nov recipe, one hour)

**Held-out loss, 18 Nov eager recipe, step 150: LR 5e-5 without clipping, against LR 5e-5 with clip 1.0 and the control at LR 2e-5.** All three arms are H100, BF16-stored (18 Nov baseline: expert banks on Adam, norm scales on Muon-H; see issue 11858), with the same 20.47% replay map (identical `data.train_weights`), linear schedule, no warmup and min_lr_ratio 0.1. The no-clip run differs from the clip run only in `max_grad_norm` (1.0 → None) and the cluster (cw-us-east-02a → cw-rno2a). Lower is better.

| set | control (LR 2e-5) | LR 5e-5, clip 1.0 | LR 5e-5, no clip | no clip − control | no clip − clip 1.0 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| all (`eval/loss`) | 0.6115 | 0.6103 | 0.6070 | -0.0045 | -0.0033 |
| SFT (`eval/sft/loss`) | 0.5093 | 0.5022 | 0.4978 | -0.0114 | -0.0044 |
| SFT source macro | 0.5368 | 0.5299 | 0.5253 | -0.0116 | -0.0046 |
| replay pretrain (`eval/replay/loss`) | 0.8514 | 0.8639 | 0.8631 | +0.0117 | -0.0008 |
| pretrain c13q3 | 0.3489 | 0.3551 | 0.3509 | +0.0020 | -0.0043 |
| pretrain c28q4 | 0.5498 | 0.5552 | 0.5557 | +0.0059 | +0.0005 |
| pretrain c30q4 | 1.7472 | 1.7718 | 1.7723 | +0.0251 | +0.0005 |
| pretrain c32q3 | 0.7599 | 0.7735 | 0.7736 | +0.0137 | +0.0001 |
| SFT agenttrove | 0.2804 | 0.2715 | 0.2715 | -0.0090 | -0.0000 |
| SFT identity-data | 1.0427 | 1.2053 | 1.1584 | +0.1157 | -0.0469 |
| SFT nemotron_sft_v3 macro | 0.5057 | 0.4778 | 0.4779 | -0.0278 | +0.0001 |

**Did clipping act, and do the two training curves match?** Read from W&B for both LR 5e-5 runs (150 updates each).

| question | clip 1.0 run | no-clip run |
|---|---|---|
| updates with a pre-clip total grad norm above 1.0 | 17 of 150 (updates 1-10, 13, 28, 31, 71, 101, 117, 144) | 18 of 150 |
| largest pre-clip total grad norm | 4.81 (update 2) | 9.19 (update 79) |
| median pre-clip total grad norm | 0.433 | 0.427 |
| updates where clipping changed the update (a group norm above 1.0) | 14 of 150 (updates 1-7, 9, 10, 13, 71, 101, 117, 144) | none (no clip) |
| train loss, update 150 | 0.4726 | 0.4727 |
| train loss, mean of updates 141-150 | 0.6721 | 0.6721 |

- **How clipping works here:** the optimizer (`grug_moe_muonh_v1`) clips each of its three parameter groups to norm 1.0 separately, not the total norm. In the step-150 checkpoint manifest (`opt_state`), the groups hold these parameters: AdamH holds `output_proj`; Adam holds `token_embed`, `embed_norm`, `final_norm`, the routers, router bias, attention gates and the expert MLPs (`expert_mlp` w_gate and w_up stored as `[26, 256, 2560, 1280]`, w_down as `[26, 256, 1280, 2560]`); MuonH holds the other matrices, the gated norms and the stacked `rms_attn`/`rms_mlp` weights (stored as `[26, 2560]`). So the binding count uses the group norms. In the clip run, the MuonH group was above 1.0 on 8 updates, AdamH on 13 and Adam on none. Nearly all of it is the first 13 updates plus 4 later spikes.
- **Where the numbers come from:** W&B logs `grad/norm/<parameter>` before the optimizer, so these are pre-clip norms. Each group norm is rebuilt from the 27 logged per-parameter norms, using the optimizer's own grouping rule. Their sum of squares matches the logged `grad/norm/total` within 1% on every update.
- **The loss curves are not equal step by step.** They differ on every one of the 150 updates, starting at update 1 by 0.00004 (0.79061 vs 0.79058).
  - Update 1's loss is computed before any update, so clipping cannot explain that first gap. It comes from the different cluster and executable, not from clipping.
  - Clipping can act from update 2 on. Mean absolute gap over updates 2-150 is 0.00034, and 12 updates differ by more than 0.001. The largest gap is 0.0044, at update 79, where the no-clip run had its one large spike (MuonH group norm 9.00 and Adam group norm 1.50, against 0.23 and 0.06 in the clip run).
- **Reading, not a conclusion:**
  - Clipping bound on 14 of 150 updates, mostly in the first 13. Train loss ended the same to the third decimal.
  - On held-out sets, no clip is 0.003-0.005 lower on all, SFT and SFT macro than clip 1.0. Replay pretrain, Nemotron and agenttrove are within 0.001.
  - Identity-data is 0.047 lower without clipping. It rests on 8 held-out packed sequences, and every arm drew 3 identity sequences in training (method caveat: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11783#issuecomment-7056481299).
    - **Correction (21 Nov):** updated the identity draw count from `1` → `3` packed sequences in 150 updates; the earlier realized-mix tool listed data sources in sorted order, whereas training uses config order (`MixtureDataset` insertion order).
  - These are single runs. The clip pair also crosses clusters, so a 0.003 gap is not separable from cross-cluster numeric noise without a repeat.
- **Weights:**
  - control (LR 2e-5): `s3://marin-us-east-02a/tmp/ttl=30d/long-loop-436/base-start-20261118/control-eager/checkpoints/step-150` ([Filer](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-02a%2Ftmp%2Fttl%3D30d%2Flong-loop-436%2Fbase-start-20261118%2Fcontrol-eager%2Fcheckpoints%2Fstep-150))
