spillover_issues.author: hammer
spillover_issues.body:
## TL;DR

Add loop guards for agent traces at four layers: SFT data filters, wait demonstrations, an episode stop on stalls, and a loop metric in evals. Then test the RL and decoding guards Marin already has. The design follows IFM's [`repetition_check.py`](https://github.com/ifm-ai/process_entry/blob/main/repetition_check.py) and the K2-Horizon results ([arXiv 2611.21003](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.21003v1)). The full survey of Marin's current loop guards, with citations, is [here](https://gistpreview.github.io/?3d44de572b8babfc08f96ac90a05b109).

## Background

- **SFT filter (main).** The only agent-loop filter is `has_stalled_tool_call` in `lib/marin/src/marin/datakit/chat_normalize.py`, added in #9259. It drops a record on the third identical tool call after two identical replies, within one user turn, and fired on 101 of 210,031 sampled conversations.
  - It misses Terminus-2 traces, because terminal output is stored as user turns and each one resets the counter.
  - It misses spread-out repetition.
- **Ending episodes (missing).** Nothing ends an episode when the agent repeats itself. The rolloutengine stops only at turn, token or time limits. Terminus-2's `turn_callback` can return EARLY_TERMINATION, but no callback uses it.
- **RL penalties (unused).** Vendored SkyRL has two loop penalties, both off by default. The loop-credit penalty was swept in #9599 and no strength stood out. No recipe enables the antithrash penalty for repeated actions.
- **Doom loops (in flight).** #9691 and #12240 target repeated token suffixes at the end of a response. They don't cover repeated actions, and `loop_audit.py` lives only on branch `benfeuer/mochi-doom-ftpo`.
- **Evals (no metric).** There is no standing loop metric. #7743 measured median exact-duplicate tool-call fractions of 20–37%, but only once.
- **IFM's evidence.**
  - RL cut exact repeats inside Terminal-Bench interrupt loops from 61.8% to 0.3%. Trials with a loop barely changed, from 12.9% to 11.6%.
  - SFT demonstrations of waiting after unchanged output brought interrupt loops below 1%. In IFM's midtraining data, the agent waited 0 times out of 446 such moments.

## Proposed work

1. **IFM-style rules in `chat_normalize.py`.**
   - Reject 8 consecutive identical name+args tool calls, whatever the replies.
   - Reject a call that occurs at least 10 times, accounts for at least 30% of assistant turns, and appears in a run of at least 3 identical calls.
   - For Terminus-2 records, reject at least 8 consecutive identical normalized assistant messages when one preceding observation accounts for at least 80% of the run.
   - Keep #9259's exemption for retries that get a different reply.
   - Report fire rates per source, and hand-check a sample for precision.
2. **Wait demonstrations.**
   - Audit the SFT and midtraining mixes for what the agent does after unchanged terminal output.
   - Add Terminus-2 rows that wait or poll on long-running commands, next to the recovery rows from #10888.
   - Generate them in a real-clock environment, because ShellSim sleeps take no wall time (#10159).
3. **Stall stop in the rolloutengine.**
   - Add a stop reason such as `REPEAT_STALL` that fires after 3 consecutive identical action batches with identical observations.
   - Grade the task anyway, so work done before the stall still earns credit.
   - Add it to the #12190 port list, and either confirm or remove the "thrashing detector" that the #6341 checklist marks done.
4. **Loop metrics in evals.**
   - Merge `loop_audit.py` to main.
   - Add to the #10197 eval policy: loop count and upper bound, the exact-duplicate tool-call fraction (the #7743 method), and an interrupt-loop count on Terminal-Bench.
   - Report repeats inside loops and the share of trials with a loop separately.
5. **Antithrash ablation.**
   - Enable `antithrash` on one agentic RL recipe.
   - Add an option to apply it only to otherwise-correct trajectories.
   - Track both measures from item 4.
6. **Decoding checks.**
   - Run a paired comparison of `repetition_penalty` 1.0 against 1.1 on the snowball-sft eval and the curriculum-RL policy.
   - Land #12254 with a full set of stop tokens.

## Done when

- [ ] `chat_normalize.py` has the three IFM-style rules with tests, and per-source fire rates are posted here.
- [ ] A wait-behaviour audit of the SFT and midtraining mixes is posted, and a wait-demonstration source is in the SFT mix.
- [ ] The rolloutengine records a repeat-stall stop reason, and the #6341 "thrashing detector" entry is confirmed or corrected.
- [ ] Eval reports show loop counts, the duplicate tool-call fraction, and the Terminal-Bench interrupt-loop share.
- [ ] Antithrash ablation results are posted with both loop measures.
- [ ] Results of the paired `repetition_penalty` test are posted, and #12254 has merged.

Related: #9259, #9599, #9691, #12240, #7743, #10197, #12190, #6341, #10888, #10159, #12254.

🤖 # Research

`has_stalled_tool_call` checks three identical calls with identical replies only within one user turn; the Terminus converter stores terminal observations as user messages, so that counter resets between shell steps. The native RolloutEngine records turns and stop reasons, then grades after the harness exits; it has no repeat-stall reason. [#12167](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/12167) has merged, while [#12240](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/12240) measures token suffix loops separately.

**Relevant code**
- [`chat_normalize.py#L144-L174`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/bf4b85caa09586d287b503bfa3e9f9d19393424b/lib/marin/src/marin/datakit/chat_normalize.py#L144-L174) — current within-turn rule
- [`download/terminus.py#L77-L123`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/bf4b85caa09586d287b503bfa3e9f9d19393424b/lib/marin/src/marin/datakit/download/terminus.py#L77-L123) — terminal output becomes user message
- [`recorder.py#L250-L318`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/bf4b85caa09586d287b503bfa3e9f9d19393424b/lib/rolloutengine/src/rolloutengine/recorder.py#L250-L318) — transitions and observations
- [`engine.py#L216-L255`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/bf4b85caa09586d287b503bfa3e9f9d19393424b/lib/rolloutengine/src/rolloutengine/engine.py#L216-L255) — harness exit and grading
- [`agents/terminus/agent.py#L986-L1012`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/bf4b85caa09586d287b503bfa3e9f9d19393424b/lib/rolloutengine/src/rolloutengine/agents/terminus/agent.py#L986-L1012) — command observation loop

# Proposed Fix

1. Define one action identity (tool name plus canonical arguments), observation identity, and Terminus message normalization against saved traces. Audit the three proposed thresholds in report-only mode across each SFT source. Publish source counts, sampled true/false positives, and the decision on how changed replies interact with the eight-call rule before filtering data.
2. Add the three filters at chat normalization, with separate counters and tests for user-message observations, nonadjacent repeats, changed replies, parallel batches, and final tool calls. Rebuild affected source artifacts only after the precision audit; link the filter PR `Part of #12264`.
3. Add a `repeat_stall` stop reason to RolloutEngine when three completed action batches and their observations match. End before the next model request and use the existing grading path so completed work keeps its score. Test changing observations, timeout precedence, and a scored stall without fabricated model turns; add the behavior to [#12190](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/12190) and verify the claim in [#6341](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/6341).
4. Count what the agent does after unchanged terminal output in the pinned SFT and midtraining mixes. Add a real-clock Terminus wait/poll source beside [#10888](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10888)'s recovery rows, then publish source identity, row count, and a hand audit that the waits actually allow time to pass.
5. Port `loop_audit.py` from the [#12240 branch](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/benfeuer/mochi-doom-ftpo) as a reviewed, reusable metric. Pin loop and duplicate-call denominators, report both repeats inside loops and trials with a loop, and add Terminal-Bench interrupt-loop counts to the eval report and [#10197](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10197). Baseline these metrics before any training intervention.
6. With that baseline fixed, run one antithrash ablation (including the correct-trajectory-only variant) and paired `repetition_penalty` 1.0/1.1 evals on identical prompts and decoding budgets. Report task scores, loop measures, and sampling settings together. [#12254](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/12254) is currently a finish-reason PR with an open turn-boundary stop-token review finding; resolve that finding and verify the full stop-token set before treating it as a decoding guard.

These are separate data, runtime, eval, and experiment changes. Each stage can land as a reviewable PR or published measurement without claiming the full issue is done.

## TL;DR

Measure exact repetitive tails in Mochi SFT step 400407, then test whether online FTPO can halve per-domain incidence while retaining native task correctness. Baseline measurement precedes training.

## Description

Adapt the [Dr. Doom campaign](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9691) to Mochi. Preserve the exact tail-loop detector and FTPO objective. Use TP1/BF16 serving and Mochi's MuonH/R3 training path. The fixed, hashed evaluation panel covers math, instruction following, coding, reasoning_gym, structured outputs, and STEM MCQ. All graders are programmatic and fail closed.

## Hypothesis or Goal

For each target domain, obtain a post-training loop upper bound no greater than half its confirmed baseline count on identical prompts. Extend low-incidence 32K cohorts from 128 to 256; fewer than 10 confirmed loops after extension makes a domain non-target. Non-target upper bounds may increase by at most three. Per-domain correctness may lose at most max(3, 5% of N) passes; pooled correctness may lose at most 2% of the panel.

The issue defines a bounded FTPO experiment, but no baseline counts, frozen panel, logbook, or training result is published yet. The linked source branch currently returns 404. The prior [Dr. Doom campaign](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9691) found that a short-tail detector missed longer exact cycles and that a smoke can exit successfully without an optimizer update. Pin the step-400407 checkpoint, runtime and grader revisions, TP1/BF16 serving configuration, sampling parameters, and prompt IDs and hashes before choosing target domains. Pin the final full-response exact-suffix detector semantics from #9691 and test their period cap, eight-repeat rule, generation masks, length stops, and unassessed-response accounting on saved examples.

Report unassessed generations and length stops separately, preserve the best export and exact launch/evaluation artifacts, and record negative results before deciding whether another update is justified.

spillover_issues.author: penfever
spillover_issues.body:
We believe that formal verification is essential for open source models to get better at math, and better generally! Lean, a popular formal verification language primarily used for mathematical proofs, is one of the most popular avenues for this kind of improvement. We don't have RL data we trust for Lean, nor do we have evals we trust. Marin needs both in order to continue improving in this domain.

cc @Robertboy18

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖
# Research

Marin already grades Nemotron RLVR1 Lean responses with a pinned Lean 4.12/Mathlib compiler ([#10080](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10080), [#10088](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10088)). That establishes a reward path for those rows, but not an audited training corpus or held-out theorem-proving eval. [#10214](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10214) excluded Lean from its mixed RLVR runs because Iris task pods could not start the Docker task machine; the [current eval policy](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10197) lists no Lean proof benchmark.

**Relevant code**
- [lean_grade.py](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/post_training/task_curation/datasets/nemotron_ultra/lean_grade.py) — current compiler-backed reward.
- [lean.Dockerfile](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/post_training/task_curation/datasets/nemotron_ultra/lean.Dockerfile) — pinned toolchain and Mathlib.
- [lean_compiler.py](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/vendor/skyrl/skyrl-gym/skyrl_gym/lean_compiler.py) — task-local execution path.
- [proofpile.py](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/datasets/proofpile.py) — existing pretraining corpus to check for overlap.

# Proposed Fix

1. **Freeze the eval first.** Inventory candidate Lean problem sets and record licenses, source revisions, theorem IDs, proof provenance, and required toolchains. Create public development and sealed test manifests; check statement/proof overlap against RLVR1, Proof-Pile 2, and proposed training sources. Specify prompts, token and time budgets, pass@1/pass@k, and how compiler failures and missing scores enter the denominator. Done when pinned reruns reproduce the same task IDs and verdicts.
2. **Audit the verifier.** Reuse the compiler path with controls for invalid proofs, `sorry`/`admit`, changed statements, extra axioms, and timeouts. Review a stratified sample of accepted and rejected attempts independently, publish disagreement counts, and resolve reward exploits before training. Keep the compiler and Mathlib revision identical between data validation and eval.
3. **Curate RL tasks.** Normalize licensed Lean statements and headers into provenance-bearing task records, deduplicate by theorem and near-duplicate text, and compile reference proofs where provided. Keep eval problems and their proof variants out of training. Resolve the Iris task-pod execution gap seen in #10214, then run a real task-session smoke test. Done when each released row has a source, toolchain pin, verification outcome, and contamination decision.
4. **Measure transfer.** Run pinned baseline models on the frozen eval, reporting pass@1/pass@k with uncertainty, per-source scores, and compiler/error rates. Compare a small Lean RL pilot against its starting checkpoint on the same eval and publish the dataset and run revisions. Expand the data or training budget only if the audited reward and held-out scores support it.

Thanks for the cc! I fully agree, and I'd be very happy to help with this and lead the effort. I've been working on various LLM + Lean projects, so this lines up well.

One thing I'd do early is move off Lean 4.12 and its October 2024 Mathlib to a more recent release, and use the same pin for both the RL data and the evals. How would you like me to put together a detailed plan? I can write it up here, or we could chat on Discord first if that's easier :)

comments.author: Robertboy18
comments.body:
Thanks! I looked through what's out there, and a few things seem worth starting from:

- **One Lean version for data and evals.** I'd suggest v4.34.1: it has the fix for a kernel bug that allowed an axiom-free proof of `False` (leanprover/lean4#14576), and it's what Prime Intellect's Lean environments and openai/math use.
- **Evals:** [PutnamBench](https://github.com/trishullab/PutnamBench), [miniF2F (DeepMind fork)](https://github.com/google-deepmind/miniF2F) and [ProofNet-Verified](https://github.com/marcusm117/ProofNet-Verified), with [Lean Eval](https://github.com/leanprover/lean-eval) as a hard ceiling.
- **RL data:** [Goedel RL_dataset_V2](https://huggingface.co/datasets/Goedel-LM/RL_dataset_V2), [NuminaMath-LEAN](https://huggingface.co/datasets/project-numina/NuminaMath-LEAN) and [Kimina](https://huggingface.co/datasets/project-numina/Kimina-Prover-Promptset), plus [mathlib-tactics](https://huggingface.co/datasets/mathlib-initiative/mathlib-tactics) for SFT warm-up.
- **Environments:** [Prime's Lean environments](https://github.com/PrimeIntellect-ai/prime-envs/tree/main/environments/lean) have the strictest grader I found and already filter these datasets for v4.34. Their env code only runs on Prime's VMs, but the image and checker are Apache-2.0, so we could reuse them in Harbor. [FineEnvs/openai-math](https://huggingface.co/datasets/FineEnvs/openai-math) runs on Harbor today.

One gap: nobody has the code-verification benchmarks (VERINA, CLEVER, Vericoding, FVSpec) on one version yet. I have them internally and will make them public once I've upgraded them all to v4.34.1. Which track would you like first?

After that, we can push further on getting more data and/or doing some RL?

comments.author: XiaoyuanWang111
comments.body:
🤖 A reward-floor check on the NuminaMath-LEAN training tasks from #11095, before the first Lean RL run. I rebuilt the 4,035 tasks with the recipe's own `row_contract` on main `2bf3f721c`, drew 1,000 at random and compiled fixed replies against each statement in the grader's proof-term form, with the grader image's Lean v4.34.1 and Mathlib `d13f23b`. 795 of the 1,000 were graded in the time I had (the first 300 in order, then a random part of the other 700); the shares weight the two parts by their size.

| Fixed reply | Tasks proved (95% interval) |
|---|---|
| `grind` | 19% (16.5-22%) |
| `first \| (rfl; done) \| (decide; done) \| ... \| (exact?; done)` over 15 tactics | 25% (22-28%) |
| any one of `simp`, `norm_num`, `decide`, `omega`, `linarith`, `exact?`, `aesop`, `trivial`, `rfl` | 17% (14-19%) |

So about 1,000 of the 4,035 tasks give reward 1 to one constant reply. On ProofNet-Verified, `simp`, `simp_all`, `aesop`, `grind`, `tauto`, `ring` and `exact?` proved 49 of 366 rows through the grader (13%, in my #10879 review); those seven prove 24% here. Every task has a compiling human proof, so none is false, but in a random 200, `grind` derives `False` from the hypotheses of 4.

I read 20 of the proved tasks. 16 are faithful but easy: final computations such as `algebra_15505` (`gcd 2835 8960 = 35`), and answers that follow from the stated equations. 4 state less than their problem:

- `algebra_13062` (`fbf349fa`): `h : ∀ x, x ≠ 3 ∧ x ≠ -5 ∧ ...` is false at `x = 3`.
- `algebra_160868` (`ec81e530`): `∀ n, F n = F (n - 1) + F (n - 2)` over ℕ forces `F 0 = 0`, but `F 0 = 1`.
- `algebra_235251` (`f7637b05`): the equation that solves the frog problem is a hypothesis.
- `Number_Theory_640629` (`ed0dad30`): the egg problem became a statement whose inner condition cannot hold, so it is true for every `m`.

Two more have contradictory hypotheses: `algebra_174839` (`c1528388`) and `combinatorics_609372` (`3962696e`, `r = 50`, `b = 50`, `r - b = 5`).

A group in which every sample succeeds has no advantage, so most of these tasks only cost rollouts, and the vacuous ones reward a reply that ignores the problem. Grading the `first | ...` reply once per task at curation takes about 4 s a task in a batch. Would a filter, or a difficulty tag for the curriculum, be useful? I can add either to the recipe.

comments.author: Robertboy18
comments.body:
Thanks Xiaoyuan, this is really useful! Yes please, I think both would help:
- Drop the tasks whose hypotheses already prove `False` (your `grind` check), since any reply gets reward there.
- Tag the rest by whether the fixed `first | ...` reply proves them, so the selection recipe can drop or downweight the easy ones. Small models may still learn from them, so a tag seems better than a hard filter.

The ones that state less than the problem, like `algebra_235251` and `Number_Theory_640629`, won't show up in either check. On #11526 we ran the human problem text through a judge against the Lean for every row, and it caught a lot of these, so I'm happy to run the same thing over the 4,035 and send you the list :)

comments.author: XiaoyuanWang111
comments.body: Thanks Robert, will do. I'll open a PR that adds both to the NuminaMath-LEAN recipe: tasks where `grind` derives `False` from the hypotheses are dropped, and every other task is tagged with whether the fixed `first | ...` reply proves it, so the selection recipe can drop or downweight the easy ones. Your judge list would be great, since neither check sees the statements that say less than their problem; I'm happy to fold it in once you have it.

comments.author: Robertboy18
comments.body:
Here's the judge list for the 4,035 NuminaMath-LEAN tasks. Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol each read the problem and the Lean statement, and 460 tasks (11.4%) are flagged by both. A third pass sorted them by what matters for RL:
- 133 vacuous: the hypotheses can't hold or allow a degenerate case, e.g. `algebra_215374` assumes `x + 1/x = √2` over ℝ, and `number_theory_608455` lets `a = 0` with `0⁻¹ = 0`
- 116 give the answer or a key step away as a hypothesis, e.g. `geometry_609751` assumes Ptolemy
- 153 weaker but still true and non-trivial: a bound without attainment, one direction, or missing uniqueness
- 54 state a different claim, like wrong data or a wrong definition
- 4 the third pass thinks are fine

I'd drop the first two (249 tasks) and maybe tag the other two. Both judges flagged all 6 of your examples and passed `algebra_15505`, and 11 of 12 random flags I checked by hand were clearly right (1 borderline). Full list below :)

comments.author: BirgerMoell
comments.body:
Related to steps 2 and 3: we've built an open set of Lean tasks with a verifier built to resist reward exploits. It may be a useful input, especially for the verifier audit and the RL curation.

Lean Arena (Renaissance Labs): https://huggingface.co/datasets/RenaissanceLabsEU/math, with a map of the 63 MSC areas and their Mathlib coverage at https://math.renaissancelabs.eu/

Tasks: 972 tasks in 9 environments (inequalities, group theory, linear algebra, real analysis, finite sums, and more). Each environment has 84 train and 24 eval tasks at three difficulty levels. A model fills in Solution.lean, or writes a definition. The tasks are in Harbor format.
Generated, not scraped: every task comes from a seeded generator, so each row has a seed, a family and a difficulty, and the dataset can't overlap with miniF2F, PutnamBench or Proof-Pile. Fresh seeds give unlimited new tasks.
Verifier: Verify.lean loads the hidden reference and the submission and compares kernel terms. It requires that the task's own definitions are unchanged, that the statement matches exactly, and that the proof uses only propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound. We also re-check with leanchecker. sorry, native_decide, a user axiom, a changed definition and a weakened statement are all rejected, and tools/verifier_cheats.py tests each of these.
Container check: we ran it with no network on one held-out task per environment. The reference solution scored 1.0 and the untouched start file scored 0.0. Grading takes about 2.5 minutes per task, mostly importing Mathlib several times.

Caveats:

It's on Lean 4.29.1 with Mathlib 5e932f97, not v4.34.1. The generators don't depend on the version, but moving would mean regenerating and re-running the self-tests.
We have no model baseline yet. One automation tactic closes 15 of 192 sampled proving tasks, which is a floor for how much needs no real proof, not a model score.
The eval split is in distribution (same templates, different seeds). It's good for RL practice, but it's not a general theorem-proving benchmark and shouldn't replace miniF2F or PutnamBench.

We can discuss this more in the math channel.

spillover_issues.author: chrismc91
spillover_issues.body:
Marin cannot serve or evaluate `reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B` because the locked `transformers` 5.12.1 cannot load its tokenizer. Marin loads the tokenizer in its own environment in two places: `read_tool_chat_template` (`lib/marin/src/marin/inference/model_preparation.py`), called when vLLM starts, and the evaluation task worker (`lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/task_worker.py:210`). `AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained` reads the model config first. `transformers` 5.12.1 does not register model type `beam`, and its fallback config fails RoPE validation on Beam's `rope_parameters`, which sets `full_attention` to `null`:

```
File ".../transformers/models/auto/tokenization_auto.py", line 720, in from_pretrained
File ".../transformers/configuration_utils.py", line 844, in from_dict
File ".../transformers/modeling_rope_utils.py", line 795, in validate_rope
AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'get'
```

vLLM itself serves Beam: upstream vLLM 0.34.0 registers `BeamForCausalLM` and its own `BeamConfig`. This blocks Beam 1.0 as a Tier 3 comparison model for the Nov 30 eval policy.

Reproduce:
1. `uv run python -c "from transformers import AutoTokenizer; AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained('reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B', revision='877a5d6973c6ae6a55335483002c06717662d23c')"` in a Marin checkout fails as above.
2. The same call succeeds with `transformers` 5.16.1 and 5.22.0.

Expected: Marin loads Beam's tokenizer, so Beam can be served and evaluated.

Upgrading the lock is blocked: `transformers` 5.16.1 requires `safetensors>=0.8.0`, while `lib/levanter/pyproject.toml` pins `safetensors[numpy]>=0.4.2,<0.7.0`. Beam's `tokenizer_config.json` names its tokenizer class (`TokenizersBackend`), so a tokenizer load that does not read the model config would also avoid the error.

Part of #12156. cc @yonromai @dlwh @rjpower

comments.body:
🤖 **Research**

`transformers` 5.12.1 reads `config.json` before `tokenizer_config.json` in `AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained`. Beam's unregistered `beam` model type reaches fallback RoPE validation and fails before its declared `TokenizersBackend` can load. Both serving and evaluation use Levanter's shared tokenizer loader.

**Relevant code**
- [`hf_checkpoints.py#L1518`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/compat/hf_checkpoints.py#L1518) — shared AutoTokenizer call
- [`model_preparation.py#L88`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/inference/model_preparation.py#L88) — serving template probe
- [`task_worker.py#L207`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/task_worker.py#L207) — evaluation tokenizer load

**Proposed Fix**

When `tokenizer_config.json` explicitly declares `TokenizersBackend`, load that class through the shared loader before asking `AutoTokenizer` to parse the model config. Keep `AutoTokenizer` for other tokenizer classes. Add a local regression fixture with Beam's unsupported config shape and verify tokenization and special tokens.

spillover_issues.body:
**A higher-priority multi-host job cannot get capacity when a reservation is fully held by smaller, lower-priority slices.** Preemption only replaces one existing slice of the same size or larger. The autoscaler never scales down busy lower-priority slices to make room. So the job waits indefinitely, whatever its priority.

## Example (2026-11-17, reserved v4 pool, us-central2-b)

- **Demand:** a production-band (band 1) coscheduled job needing a v4-1024 slice (512 chips, 128 hosts), submitted 17:13Z.
  - Its scale group created a queued resource at 17:16:21Z. That resource was still `WAITING_FOR_RESOURCES` in GCP at 18:45Z.
  - All 128 tasks were pending with "No workers match constraints".
- **Supply:** the reservation's 1,024 chips were all in READY slices, every one running tasks. No slice was idle.

| Slice size | Ready slices | Chips | Bands of running tasks |
|---|---|---|---|
| v4-8 | 96 | 384 | batch (95), interactive (1) |
| v4-32 | 4 | 64 | batch, interactive |
| v4-64 | 4 | 128 | batch, interactive |
| v4-128 | 1 | 64 | batch |
| v4-256 | 1 | 128 | batch, interactive |
| v4-512 | 1 | 256 | batch |

- Every running task was in a lower band than the waiting job, yet nothing could be evicted for it.
- Removing about 512 chips of the smaller slices (for example most v4-8 slices plus the v4-128 and v4-256) would have let GCP create the v4-1024 slice.

## Why, in the code (main at f5d3c85f9e)

- **[`_preempt_coscheduled`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/f5d3c85f9e4914a48994d9a29f8c3e9104de84e0/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/scheduling/policy.py#L456-L502)** evicts **one** victim slice. That slice must have the same `device_variant` as the preemptor, strictly lower band on every member, and at least `n_required` members. Smaller slices of another variant never qualify, and several slices are never combined.
- **[`run_preemption_pass`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/f5d3c85f9e4914a48994d9a29f8c3e9104de84e0/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/scheduling/policy.py#L614-L637)** documents the same rule: a coscheduled preemptor evicts an entire slice "of the same device-variant and at least the preemptor's task count".
- **[`_preempt_coscheduled_partial_hosts`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/f5d3c85f9e4914a48994d9a29f8c3e9104de84e0/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/scheduling/policy.py#L550-L565)** frees hosts by evicting solo co-tenants, but only on hosts of the gang's own variant, so it needs those workers to exist first.
- **Autoscaler scale-down is idle-based only** ([`scaling_group.py` idle threshold](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/f5d3c85f9e4914a48994d9a29f8c3e9104de84e0/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/autoscaler/scaling_group.py#L125-L135)).
  - Routing orders groups by the group's config priority ([`route_demand`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/f5d3c85f9e4914a48994d9a29f8c3e9104de84e0/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/autoscaler/routing.py#L715-L725)), not by the priority band of the demand.
  - Nothing releases busy lower-band slices to free reservation quota for higher-band demand that a group cannot satisfy.

The rule is deliberate: "same-variant + slice-shaped" avoids large/small thrashing. But inside a fixed reservation, it means priority cannot reclaim capacity that has been fragmented into smaller slices.

## Proposed direction

When a higher-band demand stays unmet because its group cannot get capacity in a reservation, the autoscaler should drain lower-band slices in the **same reservation** until enough chips are free for the requested slice:
- Preempt their tasks through the normal preemption path, then delete the slices.
- Prefer the lowest band, then the youngest tasks.
- Gate it on the demand having been unmet for a minimum time, and stop as soon as the chips are free, to limit thrashing.
- Record each drain (preemptor, victims, chips freed) so it can be audited.

---

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 # Research

The current preemption pass binds a coscheduled preemptor to workers freed by one same-variant slice, so it cannot combine smaller v4 slices into a new v4-1024 allocation. The autoscaler routes by scale-group priority, does not carry the pending job's band in `DemandEntry`, and scales down only idle slices; `quota_pool` groups quota failures but has no shared chip ledger. [#6818](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/6818) and [#6819](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/6819) developed the ledger, drain lifecycle, and cross-variant pass, then closed unmerged after inactivity. I found no open PR for this issue or mechanism.

**Relevant code**
- [`policy.py#L460-L503`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/scheduling/policy.py#L460-L503) — one same-variant victim slice
- [`models.py#L29-L39`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/autoscaler/models.py#L29-L39) — demand lacks priority band
- [`routing.py#L710-L756`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/autoscaler/routing.py#L710-L756) — group-priority routing
- [`scaling_group.py#L647-L671`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/autoscaler/scaling_group.py#L647-L671) — detach before cloud deletion
- [`controller.py#L1021-L1072`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/controller.py#L1021-L1072) — schedule and autoscale tick ordering

# Proposed design

A production v4-1024 demand should reclaim enough chips from lower-band slices in its own reserved pool, then wait for a new v4-1024 slice to become ready. This crosses scheduling, autoscaling, slice persistence, and cloud deletion, so I would split it into reviewable stages:

1. **Pool accounting and safe drain lifecycle.** Add an explicit physical chip budget to each reserved `quota_pool` (1,024 chips for the reported `v4-reserved/us-central2-b` pool), validate that all member groups agree, and derive a per-tick ledger of live, capacity-backed creating, and draining chips. Track `WAITING_FOR_RESOURCES` requests separately because they have not acquired chips. Keep a slice tracked as `DRAINING` until cloud deletion is confirmed; make drain idempotent and retry a stuck deletion. The autoscaler must count draining chips as unavailable for new allocations and cap launches across *all* sizes in the pool. Adapt the useful parts of #6818 to the current controller.
2. **Band-aware demand and cross-size drain.** Carry the requested priority band into `DemandEntry` and admit pool launches in band order. On an autoscale tick, when a reserved-pool demand has waited at least a configurable grace period and no ready or capacity-backed creating slice of the requested shape can satisfy it, calculate the chip deficit. A queued GCP resource still `WAITING_FOR_RESOURCES` must remain eligible for a drain; reuse that request after capacity is freed. Select physical victim slices in the same pool whose *every* occupant is strictly lower band, preferring the lowest band and then youngest tasks. Skip victims with a coscheduled job spanning several slices unless its whole gang can be handled. Evict nothing unless eligible victims cover the full deficit; stop selecting as soon as they do. Commit task preemption and slice drain together on the same tick, then launch or unblock the requested shape only after GCP releases the chips. Adapt #6819's physical-slice grouping and schedule-only-tick guard; include an audit record with preemptor, victims, pool, and chips freed.
3. **Regression and rollout gates.** Use a 1,024-chip mixed-size fixture matching this issue to prove that one production v4-1024 demand reclaims exactly enough lower-band chips and eventually receives its slice. Cover equal/higher-band occupants, another pool or zone, insufficient eligible chips, a queued replacement blocked on capacity, a replacement already backed by capacity, repeated ticks, failed deletion, and a schedule-only tick. Run the Iris unit suite and repository lint/review gates, then verify on a dev controller before enabling the policy on the reserved v4 pool. No live drain or controller restart is part of this triage.

The main risk is evicting work while GCP still cannot create the replacement slice. The ledger and deletion confirmation prevent double-spending chips; the grace period and in-flight check limit repeated churn. Before enabling this for the production pool, confirm that the configured `quota_pool` maps to one fungible GCP reservation and that its physical budget is 1,024 chips.

comments.author: karansag
comments.body:
🤖 **Design for a fix (for review before code).**

## Prior work checked

- **Issue 6217** ("Higher Queues Should Preempt Across Node Types for Reserved Compute", closed as stale on 2026-08-29) asked for the same thing. Its research comment proposed relaxing the scheduler's same-variant gate on reserved capacity and left three questions open:
  1. What is a "reserved pool"?
  2. How do we stay thrash-safe?
  3. Which bands may cross?

  This design answers all three.
- Echo searches on reservation, priority and drain found no other decision. `lib/iris` docs have nothing on this.
- The config already has the pool key: every size of a `tpu_pools` entry gets `quota_pool = "<pool>/<zone>"` (`config.py:1509`), for example `v4-reserved/us-central2-b`. Groups with `capacity_type: reserved` and the same `quota_pool` draw on one reservation.

## Which component acts: the autoscaler, with the controller doing the preemption

Relaxing the scheduler gate alone does not work:
- The preemptor cannot land this tick. A v4-1024 needs a new slice, not freed v4-8 workers.
- The preempted batch tasks go back to PENDING and are re-placed on the freed workers of their own slices on the next tick, because those slices are still READY and their groups still have demand. Nothing is returned to the reservation.

The capacity owner must remove the slices. The autoscaler is the only component that knows all four facts that matter:
- the pool,
- that the preemptor's group has a slice waiting on the cloud and for how long,
- each slice's chip count,
- which slices are READY.

**Change:**
1. **`DemandEntry` gains `priority_band`.** The residual-demand builder in `scheduling/policy.py` already reads the job row.
2. **`WorkerStatus` gains `max_running_band`,** the highest band of the tasks running on that worker (none when idle). The controller already builds `WorkerStatusMap` from running tasks.
3. **New pure function `plan_reservation_reclaim(groups, demand, worker_status, now)`** in a new `autoscaler/reclaim.py`. It returns `ReclaimDecision(preemptor_job, pool, victim_slices, chips_needed, chips_freed)`.
4. **`AutoscaleResult` gains `reclaim: list[ReclaimDecision]`.** The controller folds each decision in one transaction:
   - Mark every task on the victim workers PREEMPTED, with the reason `reservation reclaim for <job> in <pool>`, through the existing preemption transition. This counts against the victim's preemption-retry budget, the same as ordinary preemption.
   - Fence those workers, then call the existing `remove_capacity`. The slices are deleted, so their chips go back to the reservation, and the cloud then fulfils the preemptor's waiting queued resource.

## Trigger (all must hold)

- **Reserved demand:** a coscheduled demand entry of band B is routed to a group with `capacity_type: reserved`.
- **Waiting on the cloud:** that group has a slice that is not READY because it is waiting on the cloud (BOOTING or REQUESTING for the queued resource).
- **Unmet long enough:** that slice has existed for at least `reclaim_min_wait`, default 10 min. A short wait usually means normal provisioning, not a full reservation.
- **No recent reclaim:** no reclaim for this pool within the last `reclaim_cooldown`, default 30 min, unless the earlier reclaimed slice has since become READY. If the cloud still cannot place after a drain (for example, the reservation is also used outside Iris), Iris does not keep killing jobs.

## Victim choice

- **Candidates:** READY slices in other groups (any size) with the same `quota_pool` and `capacity_type: reserved`.
  - Every worker of a candidate is idle or runs only bands strictly lower than B. **Equal or higher bands are never touched.**
  - A slice with even one equal-or-higher task is skipped whole.
- **Order:**
  1. Idle slices first. They cost nothing; scale-down would have taken them after the idle threshold anyway.
  2. Then the lowest band first (batch before interactive).
  3. Then fewest chips first.
  4. Then the youngest slice, so the least work is lost.
- **Stop** as soon as the freed chips reach `chips_needed`, the chip count of the waiting slice.
- **All or nothing:** if the candidates cannot reach `chips_needed`, drain nothing and record `reclaim_blocked` with the shortfall.
- **One preemptor per pool per tick:** the highest band first, then the oldest.

**Limit:** Iris does not know how many chips are free in the reservation; GCP only reports the queued resource as waiting. So `chips_needed` assumes none are free. That may drain somewhat more than strictly needed, never less. A follow-up could add an optional per-pool `reserved_chips` budget to the config and subtract live usage.

## Recording

- Every reclaim is written to the autoscaler action log (`_log_action("reservation_reclaim", ...)`), as scale-ups and scale-downs are today. The entry carries:
  - the preemptor job and its band,
  - the pool,
  - each victim slice with its chips and its jobs' bands,
  - `chips_needed` and `chips_freed`.
- `reclaim_blocked` is recorded the same way.
- Victim tasks get the preemption reason above, so `iris job` views show why they stopped.

## Tests (existing fakes; no cluster)

All pure-function tests of `plan_reservation_reclaim`, plus one controller fold test:
1. Today's case: a reserved pool full of batch v4-8, v4-32, v4-64, v4-128, v4-256 and v4-512 slices, and a production v4-1024 waiting past `reclaim_min_wait`.
   - Expect idle slices, then the smallest batch slices, until 512 chips are freed.
   - Expect no interactive slice to be drained while batch slices suffice.
2. Equal-band victims are never chosen, and a slice with one equal-band task is skipped whole.
3. Below `reclaim_min_wait`, or inside the cooldown: no reclaim.
4. Not enough lower-band chips: no drain, and `reclaim_blocked` is recorded.
5. A preemptible or on-demand pool, or a different `quota_pool`: never reclaimed from.
6. Controller fold:
   - victim tasks go to PREEMPTED with the reason, and their workers are fenced and passed to `remove_capacity`;
   - the victim jobs' preemption-retry counts go up by one;
   - the preemptor is not placed in the same tick.

## Not in scope

- Solo (non-coscheduled) preemptors.
- Preemptible pools, where freeing chips gives no guarantee.
- Any change to deployment or a live cluster.

The settings live in the autoscaler config: `reservation_reclaim.enabled` (proposed default: on), `min_wait` (10 min) and `cooldown` (30 min). Operators can tune reclaim, or turn it off, per cluster.

comments.author: karansag
comments.body:
🤖 Draft fix: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11617. It follows the design above, with two changes:
- **Off by default:** reclaim runs only for pools listed in `defaults.autoscaler.reservation_reclaim.quota_pools`.
- **Tasks fail through the worker-failure path:** a victim's tasks become `WORKER_FAILED` on their preemption budget, through the existing `_remove_worker_capacity` path, not `PREEMPTED`.

The PR lists the two choices left to the Iris owners (default off, and which bands may be victims) and the limits.

comments.author: penfever
comments.body:
🤖 **GB200 instance on cw-us-east-08a (2026-11-25): the blocked production gang is unplaceable per-pod — and Kueue preemption there is not same-shape-gated**

Context: four PRODUCTION micro210 eval rows (16-task coscheduled gangs each) sat `SchedulingGated` for hours on 08a while other users' single-host batch jobs held most of the fleet — the same symptom as this issue. I probed whether exact-shape requests force preemption on GB200.

**What the rows request** (Kueue workload `iris-pg-7e723fbd5c35df5d-0`, identical across the four): one podset of 16 pods × `nvidia.com/gpu: 8` + `rdma/ib: 8`, 32 CPU / 512Gi each, topologyRequest `preferred: backend.coreweave.cloud/leafgroup`, workload priority 1000 (production). The Iris job requests GPU variant H100: `res_device_json = {"gpu": {"variant": "H100", "count": 8}}`.

**Fleet at observation:** 204 ready nodes × 4 GB200 GPUs = 816 allocatable; ClusterQueue `iris-cq` (cw-tas flavor) usage 816/864 → 48 free GPU/RDMA quota, 0 free physical GPUs.

**Two successive pending reasons on the same workload:**

1. While quota was scarce: `couldn't assign flavors to pod set 36189f9a: ... insufficient unused quota for nvidia.com/gpu in flavor cw-tas, 80 more needed, ... rdma/ib ... 80 more needed` (128 requested − 48 free).
2. After later preemptions freed quota to 212 GPUs: `topology "multinode-nvlink-ib" doesn't allow to fit any of 16 pod(s). Total nodes: 205; excluded: resource "cpu": 65, resource "memory": 48, resource "nvidia.com/gpu": 92` — no node on 08a has more than 4 GPUs, so an 8-GPU pod fits nowhere. The H100-variant, 8-GPU-per-task shape is unplaceable on this fleet regardless of preemption.

**Probe matrix** (all PRODUCTION priority, 2-minute sleep jobs, `/benfeuer/gb200-preempt-probe-*`, UTC 2026-11-25; each cancelled or finished within ~2 min):

| probe | shape | result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| a1 | 1 task × 4 GB200, no coscheduling (the batch shape) | Placed via preemption: a batch 4-GPU pod was evicted at 10:23:30Z (`WorkloadEvictedDueToPreempted`, preemptor = the a1 pod), pod initializing 10:23:44Z, running ~10:23:47Z — ~30 s submit→running; victim requeued. |
| b1 | exact row shape: 16 × 8 GPU (H100), coscheduled leafgroup-preferred | Never placed in 7 min: reason 1, then after quota freed, reason 2. Reproduces the rows exactly. |
| c1 | 16 × 4 GB200, coscheduled hard `nvlink.domain` (one rack) | Placed via preemption: an interactive 32-pod gang (128 GB200) was atomically evicted at 10:31:16Z to free a 16-node rack; all 16 pods RUNNING in one nvlink.domain by 10:32:45Z (~2 min); victim gang requeued. |
| c3 | 32 × 4 GB200, coscheduled `nvlink.domain.sliced` (2 × 16-node slices) | Placed ~100 s with no further preemption: 16+16 pods on nvlink.domains DH1-124 and DH1-128. |

Only lower-band (batch/interactive) workloads were preempted, all with retry budgets intact.

**Code:** the same-shape rule this issue documents — `_preempt_coscheduled` evicts one victim slice of the same device variant with ≥ n_required members, every member strictly lower band (`lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/scheduling/policy.py:456-502`, gates at lines 473-495; documented in `run_preemption_pass`, lines 630-634) — governs Iris worker-fleet backends. On CoreWeave it never runs: `K8sTaskProvider.schedule` is a no-op ("Kueue owns placement, so Iris makes no scheduling decisions", `lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/backends/k8s/tasks.py:2678-2680`), and Kueue v0.18.3 admits/preempts with ClusterQueue `preemption: {withinClusterQueue: LowerPriority}` (`lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/platforms/k8s/kueue_manifests.py:409`) plus topology-aware scheduling.

**What the GB200 instance shows:**

- Production preemption on GB200/Kueue is not same-shape-gated the way the TPU instance is: production preempted single-host batch for a solo request, and evicted an entire 128-GPU interactive gang to assemble a 16-node rack for a 64-GPU request.
- Victim eviction is gang-atomic, so fragmentation surfaces as over-eviction (64 requested → 128 evicted) rather than as refusal.
- The four rows are blocked only by their per-pod shape. A relaunch at 4 GPUs/task, variant GB200 places: 16 × 4 = 64 GPUs hard-bound to one rack (`nvlink.domain`), or 32 × 4 = 128 GPUs split 2 × 16 across two racks (`nvlink.domain.sliced`) — same total compute as the current rows.

comments.author: penfever
comments.body:
🤖 **Separate finding: victim selection when production preempts for a whole rack (GB200, cw-us-east-08a)**

This is distinct from this issue's shape-awareness gap, which concerns which request shapes can preempt. This one concerns **which band gets evicted** once a placement needs a whole rack.

**Verified**
- At 10:31:16Z on 2026-11-25, probe `/benfeuer/gb200-preempt-probe-c1` ran at production as 16 × 4 GB200, coscheduled with a hard `nvlink.domain` constraint (one rack). Kueue evicted an **interactive** 32-pod gang (128 GB200) to admit it (`WorkloadEvictedDueToPreempted`, preemptor and preemptee path `/iris-cq`). All 16 probe pods were running in one NVLink domain by 10:32:45Z.
- The evicted job ended `worker_failed` with `preemptions=1`, `cosched_failed=31` and `preempted=1`. Its owner later resubmitted it as a resume.
- At the same time, roughly 230 single-node **batch** jobs (4 GB200 each) were running on 08a.
- Our ClusterQueue uses `preemption: {withinClusterQueue: LowerPriority}` (`lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/platforms/k8s/kueue_manifests.py:409`). Batch and interactive are therefore equally eligible victims for a production preemptor. No setting prefers the lowest band.
- Eviction is gang-atomic: a 64-GPU request cost 128 GPUs of eviction.

**Inferred, not yet verified**
- The batch pods were spread one per node across many racks, interleaved with other non-evictable work, so no single rack could be freed by evicting batch alone. The interactive gang occupied whole racks, so evicting it was the only one-step way to free a full rack.
- A per-rack occupancy snapshot at 10:31Z would confirm or refute this. I didn't capture one.

**Consequence**

Any rack-shaped production job on 08a can evict another user's interactive gang even while batch capacity is available elsewhere. That covers multi-node RL, rack-bound eval serving, and placement probes. The probe here was ours, and our probes now run at batch or interactive only. That doesn't protect against legitimate rack-shaped production jobs.

**Possible directions (policy call for Iris/Kueue owners)**
- A Kueue preemption or fair-sharing policy that exhausts lower-band candidates before higher ones, with rack-aware candidate selection.
- Requiring production rack requests to fail over to `nvlink.domain.sliced` before evicting interactive gangs.
- Surfacing the expected victim set before admission, so the submitter can choose.
